Question 35Incorrect

Northbridge Bureau needs to let a newly created IAM user upload course materials to an S3 bucket named northbridge-course-materials, at an education technology company headquartered in Austin, Texas. The bucket uses server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) as its default encryption setting.

The development team grants the IAM user the s3:PutObject permission on the bucket, but when the application uses the IAM user's access key ID and secret access key to call the PutObject API, it receives an access denied error.

As a Developer Associate, how would you resolve this issue?

Your answer is incorrect
Correct the bucket policy of the S3 bucket to allow the IAM user to upload encrypted objects

Explanation

Incorrect. The IAM user already has the s3:PutObject permission needed to write to the bucket, so the bucket policy is not the source of the failure. The missing permission is for using the AWS KMS key tied to the bucket's default encryption setting, and a bucket policy alone cannot grant that permission. Keyword tip: a bucket policy controls access to the S3 resource, while a KMS key policy or IAM policy controls access to the cryptographic key; these are separate permission layers.
Correct the policy of the IAM user to allow the s3:Encrypt action

Explanation

Incorrect. The action s3:Encrypt does not exist in AWS. Amazon S3 does not define an API action with this name, so no IAM policy can grant it. This option is a fabricated distractor. Keyword tip: if an action name does not appear in the official IAM Action reference for a service, treat it as a fabricated distractor.
Correct answer
Correct the policy of the IAM user to allow the kms:GenerateDataKey action

Explanation

Correct. When a bucket enforces default encryption with SSE-KMS, Amazon S3 must call AWS KMS to request a data key before it can encrypt the uploaded object. The calling principal, in this case the IAM user, needs the kms:GenerateDataKey permission on the relevant KMS key, in addition to the s3:PutObject permission on the bucket. Without the kms:GenerateDataKey permission, PutObject calls fail with an access denied error, even when the S3-level permission is set up correctly. Keyword tip: an access denied error on PutObject against an SSE-KMS bucket almost always points to a missing kms:GenerateDataKey permission on the KMS key policy or the IAM policy.
Correct the ACL of the S3 bucket to allow the IAM user to upload encrypted objects

Explanation

Incorrect. Access control lists (ACLs) control coarse-grained access to buckets and objects, such as granting read or write access to specific accounts or predefined groups. ACLs do not control AWS KMS key permissions. Even with a correct ACL, the IAM user would still lack the kms:GenerateDataKey permission needed to encrypt the object with the KMS key. Keyword tip: ACLs manage S3-level access only; they never grant permission to use a KMS key.

This question tests the interaction between Amazon S3 server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions. Uploading an object to an SSE-KMS-encrypted bucket requires two separate permissions on the calling principal: s3:PutObject on the bucket, and kms:GenerateDataKey on the KMS key used for encryption, because Amazon S3 must request a data key from AWS KMS before it stores the object. Use S3 bucket policies or IAM policies to control access to the bucket itself. Use KMS key policies or IAM policies to control access to the cryptographic key, and remember that ACLs never grant KMS key permissions. When an access denied error appears on PutObject against an SSE-KMS bucket, check both the S3 permissions and the KMS key permissions for kms:GenerateDataKey, or kms:Decrypt for read operations, and also check for explicit Deny statements, service control policies, permissions boundaries, or VPC endpoint policies that might block access.

Applied example: Northbridge Bureau stores encrypted course video files in the northbridge-course-materials bucket, and a content-upload microservice runs under a dedicated IAM user. When the platform team first enables SSE-KMS on the bucket, uploads start failing with access denied errors even though the IAM user has s3:PutObject. The fix is to update the IAM user's policy, or the KMS key policy, to add kms:GenerateDataKey, which lets Amazon S3 obtain the data key needed to encrypt each uploaded video file.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/services-s3.html

Question 36Incorrect

Fairmount International must ensure that no object is written to its Amazon S3 bucket unless the object is encrypted at rest with server-side encryption using Amazon S3-managed keys (SSE-S3). The sports analytics company ingests player performance data through a custom HTTP API that calls the PutObject operation, and it needs any upload lacking the required encryption to be rejected outright.

Which solution enforces this requirement?

Your answer is incorrect
Invoke the PutObject API operation and set the x-amz-server-side-encryption header as sse:s3. Use an S3 bucket policy to deny permission to upload an object unless the request has this header

Explanation

Incorrect. The value sse:s3 is not a valid value for the x-amz-server-side-encryption header. Amazon S3 only recognizes AES256 for SSE-S3, or aws:kms and aws:kms:dsse for SSE-KMS variants. This option uses a fabricated value that Amazon S3 will not match against any real encryption type. Keyword tip: watch for header values that sound plausible but do not appear in official Amazon S3 documentation.
Set the encryption key for SSE-S3 in the HTTP header of every request. Use an S3 bucket policy to deny permission to upload an object unless the request has this header

Explanation

Incorrect. This option assumes a user-managed SSE-S3 encryption key that can be set in the request header. Amazon S3 does not expose any such key to customers. Amazon S3 generates a unique key for each object automatically and encrypts that key with a root key that Amazon S3 rotates regularly, without ever exposing the root key. Keyword tip: if an option describes setting or retrieving an SSE-S3 encryption key yourself, treat that as a sign the option misrepresents SSE-S3.
Correct answer
Invoke the PutObject API operation and set the x-amz-server-side-encryption header as AES256. Use an S3 bucket policy to deny permission to upload an object unless the request has this header

Explanation

Correct. Setting the x-amz-server-side-encryption header to AES256 on the PutObject request specifies SSE-S3. SSE-S3 uses the 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard to encrypt each object with a unique key that Amazon S3 manages. A bucket policy Deny statement can combine a StringNotEquals condition on s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption, which blocks the wrong header value, with a Null condition, which blocks a missing header entirely. Together, these two conditions guarantee that Amazon S3 rejects any PutObject request that does not include the correct SSE-S3 header. Keyword tip: the header value AES256 combined with a bucket policy Deny statement is the standard pattern for enforcing SSE-S3 on uploads.
Invoke the PutObject API operation and set the x-amz-server-side-encryption header as aws:kms. Use an S3 bucket policy to deny permission to upload an object unless the request has this header

Explanation

Incorrect. Setting the x-amz-server-side-encryption header to aws:kms requests SSE-KMS, not SSE-S3. SSE-KMS uses AWS Key Management Service to manage the encryption key, while this scenario requires Amazon S3 to manage the key. Keyword tip: the value aws:kms always identifies SSE-KMS, while the value AES256 always identifies SSE-S3.

This question tests the ability to enforce server-side encryption at rest for Amazon S3 uploads using a bucket policy with condition keys. To require SSE-S3, the x-amz-server-side-encryption header must be set to AES256 on every PutObject request. The value aws:kms requests SSE-KMS instead, and values like sse:s3 do not exist as valid Amazon S3 header values. A bucket policy that combines a StringNotEquals condition, which rejects the wrong header value, with a Null condition, which rejects a missing header, guarantees that only correctly encrypted uploads succeed.

Practical example: Fairmount International can attach a bucket policy to its player performance data bucket that denies any PutObject request unless the request includes the x-amz-server-side-encryption header set to AES256. This prevents an application bug or a misconfigured client from uploading unencrypted player data by accident. The policy applies at the bucket level, so it protects the data regardless of which application or team member sends the upload request.

Question 37Correct

Glacier Bureau, an online gaming company, batches player purchase transactions and forwards them in bulk to its internal billing reconciliation service. To meet a new data-protection requirement, every transaction batch is now encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key before it is sent for reconciliation.

After this change was deployed, engineers began seeing the application fail with a ThrottlingException error. What measures should a developer take to fix this issue MOST optimally? (Select TWO.)

Your selection is correct
Reduce the rate of requests and consider using the backoff and retry logic

Explanation

Correct. Exponential backoff and retry logic reduces the rate of AWS KMS API calls and handles throttling responses gracefully when they do occur. AWS SDKs already include automatic retry with configurable backoff settings. This makes backoff and retry a best-practice, application-level fix for throttling. Keyword tip: for throttling errors from any AWS service, client-side backoff and retry is the standard first response.
Write queries in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to track your API request usage and submit an AWS Support case to request a quota increase

Explanation

Incorrect. Tracking API usage in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights and then requesting a quota increase from AWS Support is a valid workaround. This process can now be done more directly through the AWS Service Quotas console. This approach raises the request ceiling. It does not make the application's own request pattern more efficient. Keyword tip: a quota increase changes the service-side limit. It does not fix inefficient calling behavior in the application.
Send AWS CloudTrail events generated by AWS KMS to Amazon CloudWatch Logs

Explanation

Incorrect. Sending AWS CloudTrail events to Amazon CloudWatch Logs lets Glacier Bureau see which AWS KMS API calls are happening. This is a diagnostic step. It does not reduce the number of calls to AWS KMS. It does not fix the ThrottlingException error by itself. Keyword tip: if an option only helps you observe or analyze a problem, and does not reduce or absorb the request rate, it is not the optimal fix.
Use a bucket-level key for SSE-KMS, which will decrease the requested traffic to AWS KMS, thereby avoiding the ThrottlingException error

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 bucket-level keys for SSE-KMS reduce the number of AWS KMS requests generated during S3 object encryption. This scenario does not use Amazon S3 for the transaction encryption step. The transactions are encrypted directly before being sent to the billing reconciliation service. Keyword tip: bucket keys are an S3-specific optimization. They are irrelevant when there is no S3 storage layer in the encryption workflow described.
Your selection is correct
Use the data key caching feature with the AWS Encryption SDK encryption library

Explanation

Correct. Data key caching in the AWS Encryption SDK reuses previously generated data keys instead of calling AWS KMS to generate a new key for every encryption operation. This directly reduces the number of AWS KMS API calls. Fewer API calls means less chance of hitting the throttling limit. This is especially effective for bulk encryption workloads like Glacier Bureau's transaction batches. Keyword tip: when an application performs many encryption operations against AWS KMS, data key caching is the standard performance optimization.

An AWS KMS ThrottlingException error means the application is calling the AWS KMS API faster than the current request quota allows. The correct fix combines two things: client-side resilience through exponential backoff and retry logic, and a real reduction in AWS KMS call volume through data key caching in the AWS Encryption SDK. Diagnostic steps like CloudTrail and CloudWatch Logs Insights only help you observe the problem. Requesting a quota increase only raises the ceiling without making the application more efficient. The decision logic for any throttling scenario is the same: first reduce and smooth out the calling pattern, and only pursue a quota increase afterward if the reduced call volume still exceeds the limit.

Real-world example: a gaming company like Glacier Bureau might process thousands of player purchase transactions per minute during a peak sales event. If every transaction triggers a separate AWS KMS call to generate a fresh data key, the application can quickly exceed AWS KMS request quotas during traffic spikes. By caching data keys and adding retry logic with backoff, Glacier Bureau keeps its billing reconciliation pipeline running smoothly even under heavy load, without needing to request a higher service quota.

Question 38Correct

A recent post-incident review at a mineral processing site found that a rushed AWS Lambda deployment caused a five-minute outage in the equipment-monitoring pipeline, and the team had no fast way to revert to the previous function version. To prevent a repeat, the development team at Jasperfield Holdings, which operates this pipeline across several mining sites, wants a deployment approach for its serverless Lambda functions.

The approach must route only a small percentage of traffic to a new function version and must support a rapid rollback to the previous version with minimum downtime if the deployment goes wrong.

Which of the following options should the team choose to meet this requirement?

Set up the application to use an alias that points to the current version. Deploy the new version of the code and configure the alias to send all users to this new version. If the deployment goes wrong, reset the alias to point to the current version

Explanation

Incorrect. This option configures the alias to send all users to the new version immediately. This does not meet the requirement to route only a certain percentage of traffic to the new version. If the new version fails, every user is affected until the alias is reset, which causes more downtime than a weighted rollout. Keyword tip: watch for options that send 100% of traffic to a new version when the scenario asks for partial or weighted traffic shifting.
Set up the application to have multiple aliases of the Lambda function. Deploy the new version of the code. Configure a new alias that points to the current alias of the Lambda function for handling 10% of the traffic. If the deployment goes wrong, reset the new alias to point all traffic to the most recent working alias of the Lambda function

Explanation

Incorrect. A Lambda alias can only point to a Lambda function version. An alias cannot point to another alias. This option describes a new alias pointing to the current alias, which is not a valid configuration in Lambda. Keyword tip: if an option describes an alias pointing to another alias, treat it as structurally invalid, because aliases only route to versions.
Set up the application to directly deploy the new Lambda version. If the deployment goes wrong, reset the application back to the current version using the version number in the ARN

Explanation

Incorrect. Deploying the new version directly, without an alias, sends all traffic to the new version right away. This fails the requirement to shift only a small portion of traffic to the new version. Rolling back by changing the version number in the ARN also requires updating every client or integration point that calls the function, which increases downtime and operational complexity. Keyword tip: a direct version deployment with no alias is a signal that the option does not support canary or weighted traffic shifting.
Your answer is correct
Set up the application to use an alias that points to the current version. Deploy the new version of the code and configure the alias to send 10% of the users to this new version. If the deployment goes wrong, reset the alias to point all traffic to the current version

Explanation

Correct. A Lambda alias supports weighted routing configuration. The alias can point to two versions of a function at the same time and send a specific percentage of invocation traffic to each version. This lets the team send a small percentage, such as 10%, of traffic to the new version for canary-style testing. If a problem occurs, the team updates the alias routing configuration to send 100% of traffic back to the stable version. This rollback is fast and causes minimum downtime, because the alias ARN used by callers never changes. Keyword tip: when a scenario combines a traffic-shifting percentage with a low-downtime rollback requirement for Lambda, think of an alias with weighted routing configuration.

This question tests knowledge of AWS Lambda versions and aliases as a mechanism for controlled, low-risk deployments. A version locks in a function's code and configuration at a fixed point in time and never changes after publication. An alias is a stable pointer that client applications reference; the alias can point to a single version, or the alias can split traffic between two versions using a routing configuration with assigned weights. For canary-style deployments, the team configures the alias routing configuration to send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, and if a problem occurs, the team reverts the routing weight to the stable version for a near-instant rollback with minimum downtime. Directly deploying a new version without an alias, sending all traffic to a new version at once, or configuring an alias to point at another alias are all invalid or unsafe approaches for this requirement.

Business scenario: Jasperfield Holdings can apply this pattern to its Lambda functions that process equipment telemetry from mining sites. The team publishes a new function version, points a single alias at both the stable and the new version with a 90/10 traffic split, and monitors the new version's behavior on live sensor data. If the new version produces errors or unexpected readings, the team updates the alias weights to send all traffic back to the stable version, restoring normal operation within seconds and without requiring any change on the client side.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-aliases.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-versions.html

Question 39Correct

A regional farm-monitoring mobile app run by Anchor Regional currently uses an Amazon API Gateway REST API that invokes AWS Lambda functions for photo processing, with photo metadata stored in Amazon DynamoDB. Anchor Regional, an agricultural technology company based in Des Moines, now needs to scale this application to tens of thousands of users, adding account creation, image upload, and retrieval of previously uploaded images while minimizing operational overhead.

Uploaded images range in size from 500 KB to 6 MB.

How will you design the application with the least operational overhead?

Use Amazon Cognito identity pools to manage user accounts and set up an Amazon Cognito identity pool authorizer in API Gateway to control access to the API. Set up a Lambda function to store the images in Amazon S3 and save the image object's S3 key as part of the photo details in a DynamoDB table. Have the Lambda function retrieve previously uploaded images by querying DynamoDB for the S3 key.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Cognito identity pools do not manage user accounts. Identity pools do not provide sign-up or sign-in features. API Gateway also does not support an authorizer type called an "identity pool authorizer" — this option describes a feature that does not exist. Identity pools only issue temporary AWS credentials for authenticated or unauthenticated access to AWS services. Keyword tip: any answer that pairs an identity pool with an "authorizer" in API Gateway is describing a nonexistent feature.
Your answer is correct
Leverage an Amazon Cognito user pool to manage user accounts and set up an Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer in API Gateway to control access to the API. Set up a Lambda function to store the images in Amazon S3 and save the image object's S3 key as part of the photo details in a DynamoDB table. Have the Lambda function retrieve previously uploaded images by querying DynamoDB for the S3 key.

Explanation

Correct. Amazon Cognito user pools provide a fully managed user directory. A user pool handles sign-up, sign-in, and account management without extra custom code. API Gateway can use a COGNITO_USER_POOLS authorizer to validate each user's token directly. This design stores image files in Amazon S3, which is built for large binary objects, and stores only the S3 object key with metadata in DynamoDB. This pattern keeps DynamoDB items small and keeps lookups fast. Keyword tip: "user pool" together with "S3 key stored in DynamoDB" signals the correct, low-overhead pattern for large file uploads.
Leverage an Amazon Cognito user pool to manage user accounts and set up an Amazon Cognito user pool authorizer in API Gateway to control access to the API. Set up a Lambda function to store the images as well as the image metadata in a DynamoDB table. Have the Lambda function retrieve previously uploaded images from DynamoDB.

Explanation

Incorrect. A Cognito user pool with a user pool authorizer is the correct choice for account management and API access control. However, storing the image files directly inside DynamoDB is not correct. DynamoDB enforces a maximum item size of 400 KB. The images in this scenario range from 500 KB to 6 MB, so many images would exceed that limit. Amazon S3 is the correct place to store the image files, and DynamoDB should store only the metadata and the S3 key. Keyword tip: the DynamoDB 400 KB item size limit is the signal that large binary files must go to Amazon S3, not directly into DynamoDB.
Use Amazon Cognito identity pools to create an IAM user for each user of the application during the sign-up process. Leverage IAM authentication in API Gateway to control access to the API. Set up a Lambda function to store the images in Amazon S3 and save the image object's S3 key as part of the photo details in a DynamoDB table. Have the Lambda function retrieve previously uploaded images by querying DynamoDB for the S3 key.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Cognito identity pools give temporary AWS credentials to users. Identity pools do not create individual IAM users during sign-up. Creating one IAM user per application user is not scalable. This approach adds heavy operational overhead. Identity pools also do not provide a sign-up or sign-in interface like a Cognito user pool does. Keyword tip: the phrase "create an IAM user for each user" signals a misuse of Cognito identity pools instead of a Cognito user pool.

This question tests the difference between Amazon Cognito user pools and Amazon Cognito identity pools, and the correct storage pattern for large binary files. A Cognito user pool is a managed user directory that handles sign-up, sign-in, and account management, and it can protect an API Gateway REST API through a COGNITO_USER_POOLS authorizer. A Cognito identity pool does not manage user accounts; it only issues temporary AWS credentials so users can access AWS services directly. DynamoDB enforces a maximum item size of 400 KB, so any file larger than that limit must be stored in Amazon S3, with only the S3 object key and metadata kept in DynamoDB.

Use case: Anchor Regional, an agricultural technology company, can use this pattern to let field technicians securely upload crop-condition photos from remote areas. A Cognito user pool lets each technician create an account and sign in without Anchor Regional building custom authentication logic. Photos are stored in Amazon S3, while DynamoDB stores only the photo metadata and S3 key, keeping lookups fast even as the number of users grows into the tens of thousands.

Question 40Correct

The release engineering team at Orchardvale Technologies is troubleshooting a deployment problem affecting the airline's flight-status dashboard, a static site delivered from an Amazon S3 bucket through an Amazon CloudFront distribution reachable via a custom domain. Every deployment runs through a CI/CD pipeline: after the source stage completes, an AWS CodeBuild project defined by a buildspec.yml file compiles the site and uploads the resulting static files to the S3 bucket.

The team confirms that both the S3 bucket contents and the S3 website endpoint reflect the newest build immediately after each deployment, but travelers loading the site through the CloudFront custom domain keep seeing outdated flight information.

What should the team do to fix this issue?

Your answer is correct
Invoke an Amazon CloudFront invalidation for the changed paths

Explanation

Correct. A CloudFront invalidation for the changed paths removes those objects from CloudFront's edge caches. After invalidation, the next viewer request for those paths goes to the S3 origin instead of returning a stale cached copy. A CloudFront invalidation can target specific files or use wildcards to cover an entire folder, and it forces an update regardless of the objects' configured TTL. Keyword tip: when a CI/CD pipeline updates files behind CloudFront and CloudFront keeps serving old content, add a CreateInvalidation step for the changed paths right after the S3 upload step.
Add a post-build step to resync the S3 bucket so the latest artifacts overwrite prior objects

Explanation

Incorrect. Resyncing the S3 bucket makes sure the origin holds the newest files. CloudFront edge locations can still serve previously cached objects until their TTL expires or the cache is purged. CloudFront does not automatically detect that origin content changed. Keyword tip: updating the origin alone never guarantees immediate freshness at a CDN edge; cache freshness requires cache invalidation or versioned object keys.
Modify the S3 bucket's cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) configuration to allow all origins and redeploy the files

Explanation

Incorrect. Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) configuration controls whether a browser allows client-side JavaScript to fetch resources across different origins. CORS configuration has no effect on how CloudFront caches or serves static content at the edge. Modifying CORS settings and redeploying files cannot force CloudFront to retrieve newer versions of objects it already cached. Keyword tip: CORS errors show up as browser console cross-origin fetch failures, a different symptom than CDN cache staleness.
Enable S3 bucket versioning and keep uploading files under the same keys so CloudFront eventually sees the latest version

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 versioning tracks multiple versions of an object under the same key. CloudFront caches responses by object key and query string, not by the S3 version ID. Uploading a new version under the same key does not force CloudFront to fetch the object again from the origin. The stale cached copy stays at the edge until its TTL expires or the cache is invalidated. Keyword tip: S3 versioning solves object history and rollback, not CDN cache freshness.

This question tests the difference between updating an origin and refreshing a CDN edge cache. Amazon CloudFront serves cached objects based on the object key and the configured TTL, regardless of whether the S3 origin already has newer content. Cache invalidation, using the CreateInvalidation API, console, or CLI, is the correct tool whenever deployed files change and the update must appear immediately. Object versioning, CORS configuration, and re-uploading files to S3 all solve different problems, namely object history, cross-origin browser requests, and origin freshness, and none of them purge the CloudFront edge cache.

In practice: airlines like Orchardvale Technologies often publish flight-status information that changes throughout the day, so a CI/CD pipeline for this kind of site typically adds a CreateInvalidation step immediately after the S3 upload step, targeting only the paths that changed to avoid unnecessary invalidation charges on high-traffic distributions.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Invalidation.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Invalidation_Requests.html

Question 41Incorrect

To deploy a completed batch of code updates to its AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment without any reduction in application performance or availability, Cobalt Innovations, a museum and cultural heritage foundation that operates a public digital archive platform, must select the right deployment policy. The environment includes twelve Amazon EC2 instances.

Which deployment policy is the most cost-effective choice to meet these requirements?

All at once

Explanation

Incorrect. The "All at once" policy updates every instance at the same time. This takes the whole application out of service during the deployment. This policy directly violates the requirement of no reduction in availability. Use this policy only when a full outage is acceptable, such as in a non-critical test environment. Keyword tip: "All at once" means fastest and cheapest, but it causes a complete outage.
Rolling

Explanation

Incorrect. The "Rolling" policy updates existing instances in batches. The policy does not launch any additional capacity before starting the update. This temporarily reduces the total fleet capacity and can degrade performance during the deployment. Use the "Rolling" policy when a short capacity reduction is acceptable and cost or speed matters more than maintaining full availability. Keyword tip: "Rolling" means capacity is temporarily reduced by one batch during deployment.
Your answer is incorrect
Immutable

Explanation

Incorrect. The "Immutable" policy launches an entirely new set of instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group. The new group matches the size of the current environment, so the total capacity doubles during the deployment. This approach guarantees availability and gives the safest rollback path. This approach is also the most expensive option because it requires a full parallel fleet instead of one small extra batch. Keyword tip: "Immutable" means the safest option, but it doubles capacity and cost, so it fits high-risk changes rather than cost optimization.
Correct answer
Rolling with additional batch

Explanation

Correct. The "Rolling with additional batch" policy launches one small extra batch of new instances before updating the environment in batches. This keeps the environment at full capacity the whole time, because both the old and new application versions run together briefly. Elastic Beanstalk removes the extra batch once the deployment finishes, so the extra cost is small and temporary. This makes the policy more cost-effective than doubling the entire fleet. Keyword tip: "Rolling with additional batch" means full availability is maintained with only a minor, temporary cost increase.

This question tests knowledge of AWS Elastic Beanstalk deployment policies and how each policy balances availability, deployment speed, and cost. The "All at once" policy and the "Rolling" policy both risk reduced availability or reduced capacity during the update. The "Immutable" policy guarantees full availability and the safest rollback, but it doubles the fleet size and therefore the cost. The "Rolling with additional batch" policy achieves full availability with only one small, temporary extra batch of instances, which makes it the most cost-effective choice when zero degradation is required. When you see a similar scenario, match each stated constraint, such as cost, speed, availability, or rollback safety, against the known behavior of each policy to pick the correct one.

Practical example: Cobalt Innovations runs its public digital archive platform on Elastic Beanstalk so visitors and researchers can browse historical records at any time. When the development team pushes a code update, the museum cannot allow the platform to go offline or slow down, since researchers in different time zones access the archive continuously. By choosing the "Rolling with additional batch" policy, Cobalt Innovations keeps full capacity available throughout the deployment while only paying for one extra batch of instances for a short time.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.rolling-version-deploy.html

Question 42Correct

Oakhaven Solutions, an agricultural cooperative that tracks grain shipments across its regional silos, created an Amazon DynamoDB table to support an application and provisioned read capacity units (RCU) and write capacity units (WCU) for it. The application has been running for over a year without any throttling issues. The application now requires a second type of query over the table, so the development team decided to add a local secondary index (LSI) and a global secondary index (GSI) to the table to support that use case.

One month after implementing these indexes, the table begins experiencing throttling. Upon reviewing the table's metrics, the team observes that the RCU and WCU provisioned for the base table are still sufficient.

What is most likely happening?

Adding both an LSI and a GSI to a table is not recommended by AWS best practices, as this is a known cause of throttling

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS does not discourage using a local secondary index (LSI) and a global secondary index (GSI) together on the same table. Both index types can coexist on one table without issue, as long as each index has enough throughput for its own workload. Keyword tip: watch for options that invoke a nonexistent 'best practice restriction' instead of describing a real technical limitation.
The LSI is throttling, so you need to provision more RCU and WCU to the LSI

Explanation

Incorrect. A local secondary index does not have its own provisioned throughput. A local secondary index shares the RCU and WCU of the base table. You cannot provision separate capacity for a local secondary index. Keyword tip: if a question describes provisioning separate capacity for a local secondary index (LSI), treat that option as incorrect, because an LSI always uses the base table's throughput.
Metrics are lagging in your Amazon CloudWatch dashboard, and you should see the RCU and WCU peaking for the main table within a few minutes

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon CloudWatch metrics can lag briefly, but that lag does not explain throttling that started right after adding a global secondary index (GSI) and continued for a month. The team already confirmed that the base table's RCU and WCU are sufficient. Keyword tip: rule out a metrics-lag explanation when throttling is consistent over time and correlates with a specific architecture change, such as adding an index.
Your answer is correct
The GSI is throttling, so you need to provision more RCU and WCU to the GSI

Explanation

Correct. A global secondary index (GSI) maintains its own separate provisioned RCU and WCU, independent from the base table. When the GSI does not have enough provisioned capacity, DynamoDB throttles writes and reads on the base table itself, because DynamoDB must propagate every table update to the GSI synchronously. To avoid this problem, provision the GSI's write capacity equal to or greater than the base table's write capacity. Keyword tip: when throttling appears after adding a GSI and the base table's own capacity looks fine, suspect insufficient GSI throughput.

This question tests how DynamoDB secondary indexes affect throughput and throttling behavior. A local secondary index (LSI) shares the base table's partition key and consumes the base table's provisioned RCU and WCU, so you cannot provision separate capacity for an LSI. A global secondary index (GSI) has its own partition key, its own sort key, and its own independently provisioned throughput, so insufficient GSI capacity throttles the base table's writes and reads too, since every table update must propagate synchronously to the GSI. When throttling appears after adding a new index and the base table's own metrics look healthy, check the GSI's provisioned capacity first.

Consider this scenario: Oakhaven Solutions, an agricultural cooperative, adds a global secondary index to its shipment-tracking table so member farms can query grain deliveries by region instead of only by shipment ID. If the cooperative provisions low write capacity on the new index, a spike in shipment updates during harvest season throttles writes on the main table, even though the main table's own capacity is untouched. The fix is to raise the GSI's provisioned write capacity to match or exceed the base table's write capacity.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/SecondaryIndexes.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GSI.html#GSI.ThroughputConsiderations

Question 43Correct

Fairmount Ventures runs a serverless workflow that processes reagent and lab-supply orders around the clock, using an AWS Lambda function that calls an external vendor's HTTP API to process payment for each order. The engineering team now needs a near real-time alert sent to an existing Amazon SNS topic whenever the vendor's payment API error rate climbs above 5% of the transactions processed within any given hour, so the support team can react before the lab's supply chain is disrupted.

Which solution meets this requirement with the least operational overhead?

Log the results of payment processing API calls to Amazon CloudWatch. Leverage a CloudWatch Metric Filter to look at the CloudWatch logs. Set up the Lambda function to check the output from the Metric Filter on a schedule and send a notification via the existing SNS topic when the error rate exceeds the specified rate

Explanation

Incorrect. A CloudWatch Metric Filter extracts numeric values from log entries as they arrive. In this design, the Lambda function still has to poll the metric filter's output on a schedule. Polling adds delay, so the alert is not near real-time. Building the hourly error-rate calculation from raw filtered data also requires extra custom code. Keyword tip: a metric filter turns log patterns into a metric, but pairing it with a polling Lambda function instead of a native CloudWatch alarm is a sign of unnecessary complexity and delay.
Your answer is correct
Configure and push high-resolution custom metrics to CloudWatch that record the failures of the external payment processing API calls. Create a CloudWatch alarm that sends a notification via the existing SNS topic when the error rate exceeds the specified rate

Explanation

Correct. The application can publish a custom metric directly to CloudWatch using PutMetricData every time the external payment API call succeeds or fails. A CloudWatch alarm can then evaluate the error rate over the required one-hour window and trigger the existing SNS topic automatically, with no custom polling code needed. Keyword tip: when a scenario needs threshold-based, near real-time alerting on data that AWS does not natively track, publish a custom metric and back it with a CloudWatch alarm.
Log the results of payment processing API calls to Amazon CloudWatch. Leverage CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the CloudWatch logs. Set up the Lambda function to check the output from Logs Insights on a schedule and send a notification via the existing SNS topic when the error rate exceeds the specified rate

Explanation

Incorrect. CloudWatch Logs Insights is a query engine for searching and analyzing log data on demand. It is not built for continuous polling by a Lambda function to generate near real-time alerts. Computing and comparing an hourly error-rate threshold with Logs Insights would require significant custom logic. Keyword tip: Logs Insights supports interactive troubleshooting and ad hoc analysis, not low-latency automated alarms.
Configure CloudWatch metrics with detailed monitoring for the external payment processing API calls. Create a CloudWatch alarm that sends a notification via the existing SNS topic when the error rate exceeds the specified rate

Explanation

Incorrect. Detailed monitoring only increases the sampling frequency of metrics that an AWS service already emits, such as Amazon EC2 metrics moving from five-minute to one-minute intervals. It does not apply to calls made to an external vendor's HTTP API, because AWS has no visibility into that traffic. Since no native CloudWatch metric exists for this external API, a custom metric is required instead. Keyword tip: detailed monitoring only refines the resolution of metrics a service already produces; it never creates new metrics for external systems.

This question tests the difference between CloudWatch's built-in monitoring features and the ability to publish custom metrics for events that AWS cannot see natively, such as calls to an external third-party API. Use custom metrics with PutMetricData whenever the data being tracked is application-specific or comes from an external system, and pair the custom metric with a CloudWatch alarm to get automated, near real-time threshold notifications through SNS. Reserve Logs Insights for interactive log analysis and metric filters for deriving metrics from existing log patterns; neither one is a substitute for a native alarm. The key decision point is that a polling Lambda function adds latency and unnecessary custom code, while a CloudWatch alarm on a custom metric reacts faster and needs less code to maintain.

Use case: A biotechnology research lab like Fairmount Ventures depends on a third-party vendor to process payment for time-sensitive reagent orders. If that vendor's API starts failing at a high rate, delayed detection could stall shipments needed for active experiments. By publishing a custom CloudWatch metric for each API call outcome and attaching an alarm tied to the existing SNS topic, the support team gets notified within minutes of the failure rate crossing 5%, well before the delay affects lab operations.

Troubleshooting and Optimization
Question 44Incorrect

Quarrystone Group needs to eliminate unscheduled downtime for its production database while also resolving intermittent HTTP 500 Internal Server Error responses on its critical API, a service that powers a music streaming platform delivering personalized playlists to subscribers. The API is exposed through Amazon API Gateway, integrated with an AWS Lambda function, and backed by an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance provisioned with 4 vCPUs and 32 GB of RAM.

During unpredictable spikes in listener traffic, some API calls fail, and Amazon CloudWatch Logs show "connection limit exceeded" errors during these periods.

Which solution would best fit these requirements?

Double the RAM and vCPUs of the RDS instance

Explanation

Incorrect. Increasing the RDS instance's vCPUs and RAM is vertical scaling. Vertical scaling can improve overall performance, but it does not fix the root cause, which is running out of connection slots. Changing the instance class also usually requires a reboot or a maintenance window. This reboot can cause downtime, which conflicts with the requirement of no unscheduled downtime. Keyword tip: resizing a database instance is a compute and memory fix, not a connection-management fix, and it typically causes some interruption.
Correct answer
Use Amazon RDS Proxy and update the Lambda function to connect to the proxy

Explanation

Correct. Amazon RDS Proxy sits between the application and the database. RDS Proxy pools and reuses connections, so many Lambda invocations can share a much smaller number of actual database connections. This directly fixes "connection limit exceeded" errors caused by sudden connection bursts. RDS Proxy also improves failover handling and requires no database downtime to set up. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions Lambda, RDS, and connection exhaustion errors together, RDS Proxy is almost always the intended solution.
Use AWS Lambda to create a connection pool for the RDS instance

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda execution environments are temporary. Many Lambda invocations can run at the same time, and each invocation can open its own database connection. Building a connection pool inside the Lambda function code does not stop this problem, because each separate execution environment still creates its own pool. This approach also adds extra complexity and processing overhead to the function code. Keyword tip: when a serverless compute service needs shared, managed database connections, look for a dedicated proxy layer instead of in-code pooling.
Your answer is incorrect
Implement auto-scaling for the RDS instance based on connection count

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon RDS does not have a native auto-scaling feature that responds to connection count. RDS supports storage auto-scaling. Aurora supports read replica auto-scaling based on metrics like CPU utilization. Neither service scales database compute capacity based on the number of open connections. Keyword tip: if an answer describes a scaling behavior that does not match a documented RDS or Aurora feature, treat it as a distractor.

This question tests how to resolve database connection exhaustion in a serverless architecture where a Lambda function connects to a relational database. Amazon RDS Proxy is built specifically to pool and share connections across many concurrent Lambda invocations. RDS Proxy reduces connection overhead on the database and improves resilience and failover behavior without requiring downtime. Application-level pooling inside Lambda, connection-based auto-scaling (a feature RDS does not support), and vertical scaling of the DB instance either fail to fix the root cause or introduce unwanted downtime. The correct decision logic is to identify whether the bottleneck is the number of open connections or raw compute capacity; RDS Proxy is the standard AWS-recommended fix when the bottleneck is connection count.

Consider this scenario: Quarrystone Group's music streaming platform experiences sudden listener surges during new album releases, causing many simultaneous Lambda invocations to query the PostgreSQL database at once. Without connection pooling, each invocation opens its own connection, and the database quickly hits its connection limit, producing the HTTP 500 errors reported by users. By placing RDS Proxy between the Lambda function and the database, Quarrystone Group can absorb these traffic spikes safely, keep the database available with no unscheduled downtime, and avoid rewriting connection-management logic inside the application code.

References:

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/using-amazon-rds-proxy-with-aws-lambda/

Question 45Correct

A client escalation revealed that several security-tool license orders were never fulfilled because a processing failure silently dropped the order notifications, with no way to retry them later. Investigating the incident, Juniper Collective, a cybersecurity consulting firm, found that its order processing system sends a notification to its licensing department whenever a customer orders a security product, and separately pushes an identical notification to a fulfillment module running on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances.

The firm needs failed messages to be re-processable at a later time, and it needs the system to scale transparently during demand spikes without any manual or programmatic provisioning of resources.

Which of the following solutions addresses this use case in the most cost-efficient way?

SNS + Kinesis

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams can ingest and fan out high-throughput real-time data. However, Kinesis requires manual provisioning of shards, or CloudWatch-based scaling of shards, unless the more expensive on-demand mode is used. The scenario requires transparent scaling without manual or programmatic provisioning at the lowest cost, so Kinesis does not meet the cost-efficiency requirement here. Keyword tip: the word "shards" and any mention of manual or automatic shard scaling signal that Kinesis is the wrong choice when true zero-provisioning, low-cost scaling is required.
SNS + Lambda

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Lambda functions can be invoked directly by Amazon SNS notifications. However, EC2 instances cannot poll a Lambda function for messages the way they can poll an SQS queue. Lambda is not a durable, pollable message store, and Lambda does not support re-processing failed messages the way a queue does. Keyword tip: when EC2 instances need to poll a message source and retry failed processing, look for SQS in the correct answer, not Lambda.
SQS + SES

Explanation

Incorrect. An Amazon SQS queue delivers each message to only one consuming application per queue. This means SQS alone cannot deliver the same notification to both the licensing department and the fulfillment module without adding extra queues or fanout logic. Amazon SES only sends emails; SES does not provide message durability, retry logic, or re-processing capability for the fulfillment workflow. Keyword tip: SQS by itself, without an SNS fanout in front of it, cannot deliver identical messages to multiple independent consumers.
Your answer is correct
SNS + SQS

Explanation

Correct. Amazon SNS can fan out one published notification to multiple subscribers at the same time. In this scenario, Juniper Collective can subscribe one Amazon SQS queue for the licensing department and a second Amazon SQS queue for the fulfillment module. Amazon SQS scales automatically to absorb bursts in order volume, and no manual or programmatic provisioning is needed. If an EC2 instance fails to process a message, the message stays in the queue, or moves to a dead-letter queue, so it can be re-processed later. Keyword tip: the words "fan out to multiple consumers," "reprocess failed messages," and "no provisioning" together point to the SNS-to-SQS fanout pattern.

This question tests the SNS-to-SQS fanout pattern. In this pattern, one SNS topic publishes a single notification, and multiple SQS queues subscribe to that topic to receive independent copies of the same message. Each SQS queue supports its own retry behavior and dead-letter handling, so a failed message can be re-processed later without affecting the other queue. Use SNS+SQS fanout when one event must reach multiple independent consumers with automatic scaling and no provisioning effort. Use Kinesis instead when the workload needs ordered, replayable streaming analytics and the team is willing to manage shard capacity or pay for on-demand mode. Avoid SQS alone when multiple independent consumers each need their own copy of a message, and avoid direct Lambda invocation when a durable, pollable queue with re-processing capability is required.

Applied example: Juniper Collective, a cybersecurity consulting firm, sells security assessment licenses to clients. When a client places an order, an SNS topic publishes one notification that fans out to two SQS queues: one queue feeds the licensing department's tracking system, and the other queue feeds the EC2-based fulfillment service that provisions the license. If the fulfillment service fails partway through processing, the message remains in its queue for automatic retry, and the licensing department's queue is unaffected, all without any manual scaling work by the Juniper Collective engineering team.

Question 46Correct

The application support team at Keystone National, a regional banking institution headquartered in Ohio, manages a customer feedback feature built into the bank's online banking portal. This feature relies on an Amazon API Gateway REST API that triggers an AWS Lambda function named keystone-national-feedback-processor to handle each submission.

The function's per-invocation performance already meets requirements, but the team must reduce the time a fresh execution environment takes to become ready, since customers notice delays during traffic spikes from promotional campaigns.

How should the team optimize the Lambda function for faster initialization?

Configure an interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink to access the Amazon API Gateway REST API with millisecond latency

Explanation

Incorrect. An interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink lets resources inside a VPC reach the API Gateway endpoint without using the public internet. This endpoint controls the network path. It does not change how long a Lambda function takes to start. Keyword tip: PrivateLink and interface VPC endpoint questions test private network connectivity, not Lambda cold-start time.
Enable API caching in Amazon API Gateway to cache the AWS Lambda function response

Explanation

Incorrect. API caching in Amazon API Gateway stores previous responses so the same request does not need to reach the backend again. API caching reduces the number of backend calls and improves perceived latency for repeated, identical requests. API caching does not reduce the Lambda function's own initialization time, and it does not help with dynamic, non-cacheable responses like unique customer feedback submissions. Keyword tip: API caching solves redundant repeated calls, not function cold starts.
Configure reserved concurrency to guarantee the maximum number of concurrent instances of the Lambda function

Explanation

Incorrect. Reserved concurrency sets aside a fixed number of concurrent execution slots for a function. Reserved concurrency also stops other functions from using that capacity. Reserved concurrency does not pre-initialize execution environments, so cold starts can still happen. Keyword tip: reserved concurrency controls scaling limits and capacity allocation, not startup latency.
Your answer is correct
Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function to respond immediately to the function's invocations

Explanation

Correct. Provisioned concurrency keeps a specified number of execution environments fully initialized and ready in advance. Because these environments are already warm, invocations run immediately without cold-start delay. Provisioned concurrency is the recommended approach for latency-sensitive, synchronously invoked APIs. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions reducing Lambda startup or cold-start latency, especially for predictable or bursty traffic, provisioned concurrency is the answer.

This question tests the difference between Lambda concurrency controls and their effect on cold-start latency. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments, so invocations get a consistent, low-latency response, which makes it the right choice for latency-sensitive synchronous APIs. Reserved concurrency only caps or guarantees the number of concurrent executions; reserved concurrency does not address initialization time. API caching and VPC endpoints solve different problems entirely: API caching reduces backend calls, and VPC endpoints provide private network connectivity, but neither of these two options affects function cold starts. When a scenario states that slow Lambda startup or cold-start latency is the bottleneck, provisioned concurrency is the correct optimization.

Use case: A regional bank like Keystone National often sees short bursts of feedback submissions right after a promotional email or app notification goes out. If the feedback-processing Lambda function needs to spin up new execution environments during that burst, customers experience noticeable delays before their submission is confirmed. By configuring provisioned concurrency on the keystone-national-feedback-processor function ahead of a known campaign, the bank keeps a pool of warm execution environments ready, so every submission during the spike gets an immediate response.

Question 47Incorrect

A recent partner audit revealed that order-status notifications were being broadcast to every integration partner instead of only the partner whose order had actually changed, raising concerns about data isolation between customers. Ironwood Continental, a mid-size enterprise software vendor that runs a multi-tenant order platform for its partners, exposes a partner-specific API for each partner through Amazon API Gateway, and all orders are processed by a single shared AWS Lambda function.

How can Ironwood Continental notify each partner regarding the status of their respective orders in the most efficient manner, without affecting other partners' orders? The solution should also be scalable to accommodate new partners with minimal code changes required.

Set up a separate Lambda function for each partner. Set up an SNS topic and subscribe each partner to the SNS topic. Modify each partner's Lambda function to publish messages with specific attributes to the SNS topic and apply the appropriate filter policy to the topic subscriptions

Explanation

Incorrect. This option creates a separate Lambda function for each partner. The shared Lambda function already processes orders for all partners without problems. Adding one Lambda function per partner increases operational overhead and duplicates code. This duplication does not provide any additional isolation benefit, because a single Amazon SNS topic with filter policies can already isolate messages per partner. Keyword tip: watch for options that multiply per-partner compute resources when a single shared resource with attribute-based routing would work just as well.
Set up a separate SNS topic for each partner. Modify the Lambda function to publish messages for each partner to the partner's SNS topic

Explanation

Incorrect. This option also creates a separate Amazon SNS topic for each partner, similar to the previous option. The shared Lambda function publishes each partner's messages directly to that partner's topic, without using filter policies at all. This design still requires creating and managing a new topic every time a new partner joins. A single topic with message attribute filtering achieves the same isolation between partners with less infrastructure to manage. Keyword tip: if a design creates separate messaging infrastructure per consumer instead of using filtering, it is usually not the most scalable choice as the number of consumers grows.
Correct answer
Set up an SNS topic and subscribe each partner to the SNS topic. Modify the Lambda function to publish messages with specific attributes to the SNS topic and apply the appropriate filter policy to the topic subscriptions

Explanation

Correct. A single Amazon SNS topic can send messages to multiple subscribers, and by default every subscriber receives every message published to the topic. To send each partner only their own order updates, the shared Lambda function publishes messages with partner-specific message attributes. Each partner's subscription uses a filter policy that matches only that partner's attributes, so the partner receives only the messages meant for them. This design isolates each partner's updates without separate topics or separate Lambda functions, and adding a new partner only requires adding a new subscription with the correct filter policy, making the design scalable with minimal code changes. Keyword tip: SNS message filtering with filter policies is the standard pattern for selective message delivery from one shared topic to multiple subscribers.
Your answer is incorrect
Set up a separate SNS topic for each partner and subscribe each partner to the respective SNS topic. Modify the Lambda function to publish messages with specific attributes to the partner's SNS topic and apply the appropriate filter policy to the topic subscriptions

Explanation

Incorrect. This option creates a separate Amazon SNS topic for each partner. Amazon SNS message filtering with one topic and per-subscription filter policies already isolates messages between partners without extra topics. Creating one topic per partner adds unnecessary management overhead. Onboarding a new partner under this design requires provisioning an entirely new topic, instead of simply adding a subscription with a filter policy. Keyword tip: a separate topic per consumer is a red flag when a filter policy on one shared topic would be simpler and more scalable.

This question tests the use of Amazon SNS message filtering to deliver different subsets of messages to different subscribers from one shared topic. When multiple consumers need only a portion of the messages published by a producer, the standard approach is to publish messages with attributes and attach a filter policy to each subscription, rather than creating separate topics or separate compute resources per consumer. Duplicating topics or Lambda functions per consumer increases operational overhead and does not scale well, because each new consumer requires new infrastructure instead of a new subscription. The correct decision logic favors consolidated infrastructure with attribute-based routing over duplicated infrastructure whenever isolation between consumers is required without adding unnecessary components.

Business scenario: Ironwood Continental processes orders for many partners through one shared Lambda function. Each partner must receive status updates only for their own orders, without seeing updates meant for other partners. By publishing messages with partner-specific attributes to one SNS topic and applying a filter policy to each partner's subscription, Ironwood Continental can onboard new partners by adding a subscription, without changing the Lambda function's code or creating new topics.

Question 48Correct

During a routine performance audit, engineers noticed that Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) was routing significantly more traffic to one instance or Availability Zone than to the others, even though the load balancer had been configured to distribute traffic equally across all instances and zones.

Sablecrest Coastal, a commercial real estate firm that runs its property-listing platform on a fleet of EC2 instances behind this load balancer, needs to determine why the imbalance is occurring and how to fix it. Why is this happening and how can it be fixed? (Select TWO.)

There could be short-lived TCP connections between clients and instances

Explanation

Incorrect. Long-lived TCP connections cause traffic imbalance, not short-lived ones. A long-lived connection keeps sending requests to the same instance it first connected to. This prevents traffic from spreading evenly to newer or less-used instances. Keyword tip: connect "long-lived connections" (not short-lived) with slow rebalancing and traffic buildup on older instances.
Your selection is correct
Sticky sessions are enabled for the load balancer

Explanation

Correct. Sticky sessions bind a client to one specific target using a cookie, such as AWSALB. Every later request from that client goes to the same instance. If some clients send more requests than others, this creates an uneven load across instances. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions cookies, session affinity, or "same target for a client," treat sticky sessions as the likely cause of uneven traffic distribution.
After you disable an Availability Zone, the targets in that Availability Zone remain registered with the load balancer, thereby receiving random bursts of traffic

Explanation

Incorrect. When you disable an Availability Zone, targets in that zone stay registered with the load balancer. The load balancer stops sending new traffic to those targets. The load balancer does not send random bursts of traffic to them. Keyword tip: link "disabled Availability Zone" with "registered but not receiving new traffic," not with unpredictable traffic bursts.
For Application Load Balancers, cross-zone load balancing is disabled by default

Explanation

Incorrect. Application Load Balancers always have cross-zone load balancing enabled. You cannot disable this setting for an Application Load Balancer. Classic Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers have cross-zone load balancing disabled by default, and you must enable it manually. Keyword tip: remember "ALB = cross-zone always enabled" versus "NLB and CLB = cross-zone disabled by default."
Your selection is correct
Instances of a specific capacity type aren't equally distributed across Availability Zones

Explanation

Correct. When instances have different capacity types and those types are not spread evenly across Availability Zones, Elastic Load Balancing can send more requests to higher-capacity instances. This behavior avoids overloading lower-capacity instances with too many concurrent requests. The result is an imbalance that comes from the uneven placement of instance types, not from a configuration error. Keyword tip: mixed instance types or capacities spread unevenly across Availability Zones is a classic cause of by-design traffic skew.

This question tests the ability to identify the real cause of uneven traffic distribution behind Elastic Load Balancing, a common troubleshooting scenario. Sticky sessions intentionally pin a client to one target using a cookie, which can concentrate load on specific instances if those clients are active. Uneven placement of different instance capacity types across Availability Zones causes Elastic Load Balancing to favor higher-capacity instances on purpose, to avoid overloading weaker ones. Long-lived TCP connections keep routing traffic to the same already-connected instance, disabled Availability Zones simply stop receiving new traffic instead of getting random bursts, and Application Load Balancers always keep cross-zone load balancing enabled by default, unlike Classic Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers.

A similar situation: a commercial real estate firm running its property-listing platform on EC2 instances behind a load balancer might notice that one Availability Zone consistently handles more requests during peak browsing hours. After investigation, the firm could find that its instances use different capacity types unevenly spread across zones, causing the load balancer to intentionally route more traffic to the stronger instances, and that sticky sessions were also enabled for logged-in agents browsing property listings, compounding the imbalance.

Question 49Incorrect

Ridgewood Federation must eliminate the capacity loss that happens during AWS Elastic Beanstalk deployments, while still reusing the instances that are currently running. The organization, a weather and climate research agency that streams real-time atmospheric sensor data into forecasting models, has noticed rising error rates and service degradation for meteorologists every time a new application version is deployed, because the deployment process temporarily removes capacity from service.

The engineering team wants to change the environment's deployment policy to one that keeps full capacity available for the entire deployment without replacing the existing fleet of instances.

Which deployment policy will meet these requirements while using the existing instances?

Immutable

Explanation

Incorrect. The Immutable deployment policy launches a completely new, separate set of instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group. Traffic only shifts to these new instances after they pass health checks. The original existing instances are never updated; they are simply terminated once the new set is confirmed healthy. Keyword tip: Immutable deployments are chosen for maximum safety and easy rollback, not for reusing or updating existing infrastructure.
Correct answer
Rolling with additional batch

Explanation

Correct. The Rolling with additional batch policy launches one new batch of instances first. This new batch replaces the capacity that would otherwise be lost. After that, Elastic Beanstalk updates the existing instances in batches, the same way the standard Rolling policy works. Full capacity stays available for the whole deployment, and the existing fleet is still the one that gets updated. Keyword tip: look for a scenario that asks for both "no capacity reduction" and "reuse of existing instances" together — this policy is the only one that satisfies both conditions at once.
Your answer is incorrect
Rolling

Explanation

Incorrect. The Rolling policy updates the existing instances in batches. It takes one batch out of service at a time to update it. This means total capacity drops for part of the deployment. This does not meet the requirement of keeping full capacity the entire time. Keyword tip: the word "Rolling" by itself, without "additional batch," always signals a temporary capacity reduction.
All at once

Explanation

Incorrect. The All at once policy updates every instance at the same time. This causes a complete, though brief, outage during the deployment. This result is the opposite of maintaining full capacity. Keyword tip: All at once is the fastest deployment option, but it is also the riskiest, so it fits scenarios that accept downtime or that involve non-production environments.

AWS Elastic Beanstalk offers several deployment policies, and each one makes a different trade-off between deployment speed, capacity during deployment, and whether existing instances or new instances are used. All at once is the fastest option, but it causes a full, brief outage. Rolling avoids replacing all instances at once but still reduces capacity temporarily, one batch at a time. Rolling with additional batch adds one extra batch of instances first, so capacity never drops, while still updating the existing fleet. Immutable and Blue/Green avoid any risk to the existing instances entirely by provisioning a brand-new set of instances, but neither of them reuses or updates the original fleet. The correct policy choice depends on matching the exact stated constraint — no capacity loss, no changes to existing instances, or fastest possible deployment — to the policy built for that specific trade-off.

Use case: A weather and climate research agency like Ridgewood Federation runs continuous data ingestion pipelines that meteorologists depend on around the clock. If a deployment temporarily reduces server capacity, incoming sensor data can be delayed or dropped, which directly affects forecast accuracy. By switching to the Rolling with additional batch policy, Ridgewood Federation can deploy new application versions without ever reducing capacity, keeping its real-time data pipeline fully operational during every release.

Question 50Correct

Novapoint Foundation must achieve sub-millisecond response times when processing high-volume trading requests inside a financial trading platform built by its engineering team, a law firm that handles time-sensitive settlement trades for corporate clients.

The platform relies on Amazon DynamoDB to store trading records. Load testing revealed that during peak usage periods, read latency spikes and the team must significantly over-provision read capacity to prevent request throttling.

Which approach would allow the developers to meet the application's latency requirements?

Your answer is correct
Use Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to cache the data

Explanation

Correct. Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, in-memory cache built specifically for DynamoDB. DAX reduces read response times from single-digit milliseconds down to microseconds for cached items. DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so the application needs only minimal code changes to use DAX. DAX also absorbs repeated read requests, which lowers the read capacity the table needs during bursty or read-heavy periods. Keyword tip: look for microsecond or sub-millisecond latency combined with reduced read-capacity over-provisioning as signals that point to DAX.
Use exponential backoff in the application code for DynamoDB queries

Explanation

Incorrect. Exponential backoff is a retry strategy that spaces out repeated requests after a throttling error. Exponential backoff helps an application recover gracefully from throttling, but exponential backoff does not reduce the read latency of successful requests. Exponential backoff also adds delay when retries happen, which can make overall response time worse during high utilization. Keyword tip: exponential backoff manages retries after throttling, it does not reduce latency.
Create a Global Secondary Index (GSI) for the trading data

Explanation

Incorrect. A Global Secondary Index (GSI) lets an application query a DynamoDB table using a different partition key and sort key than the base table. A GSI improves query flexibility for different access patterns. A GSI does not reduce the latency of read requests, and creating a GSI does not solve the throttling or over-provisioning problem described. Keyword tip: a GSI solves access-pattern and query-flexibility problems, not latency or caching problems.
Store the trading data in Amazon S3 and use S3 Transfer Acceleration

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads and downloads to Amazon S3 over long distances by routing traffic through Amazon CloudFront edge locations. This feature does not affect DynamoDB read latency or throttling. Moving the trading data to Amazon S3 would also change the application's data access pattern, which does not match the requirement to keep using DynamoDB. Keyword tip: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration solves slow S3 transfers over distance, not database latency.

This question tests the ability to choose the right tool for reducing DynamoDB read latency under high load. Amazon DynamoDB normally delivers single-digit millisecond response times, but some applications need faster, more predictable read performance without manually over-provisioning capacity. Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a purpose-built, in-memory cache that sits in front of DynamoDB and returns cached reads in microseconds, which directly reduces both latency and the read capacity the table needs. Exponential backoff only manages retries after throttling, a Global Secondary Index only adds new query patterns, and Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration only speeds up file transfers, so none of the other options address the latency or capacity problem described.

Consider this scenario: Novapoint Foundation, a law firm handling time-sensitive settlement trades, needs its trading platform to respond to read requests in microseconds so attorneys and trading partners see up-to-date settlement data without delay. By placing Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the DynamoDB table, Novapoint Foundation's engineering team can serve repeated reads from cache during peak trading windows, which cuts response time and avoids over-provisioning read capacity just to survive short bursts of activity.

Question 51Correct

Keystone Networks needs to eliminate write throttling on a DynamoDB table without increasing its provisioned throughput cost. As a sports analytics company that ingests real-time game statistics, Keystone Networks operates a busy table named KeystoneGameStats that stores game event records using the event date as the partition key.

During major game days, writes to the table are being throttled even though the table's consumed throughput stays well below its provisioned throughput.

According to AWS best practices, how can the Developer resolve the issue at the LOWEST cost?

Use an Amazon SQS queue to buffer the incoming writes

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SQS can smooth out the rate of writes over time. However, SQS adds cost. This cost includes queue charges. This cost also includes compute resources needed to poll and process the queue. SQS also adds architectural complexity. SQS does not fix the underlying hot-partition design problem. Keyword tip: buffering with a queue addresses throughput spikes. It does not address uneven key distribution. A queue is rarely the lowest-cost fix for a hot partition.
Your answer is correct
Add a random number suffix to the partition key values

Explanation

Correct. The event date partition key sends all writes for a single day to one partition. This creates a hot partition. A hot partition gets throttled even when the table's overall consumed throughput is low. Adding a random number suffix to the partition key spreads items across multiple partitions. This is called write sharding. Write sharding spreads the write load evenly. It does this at no additional cost. Keyword tip: if a table shows low overall consumed throughput but still gets throttled, suspect a low-cardinality partition key. Consider write sharding as the fix.
Increase the read and write capacity units for the table

Explanation

Incorrect. Increasing read and write capacity units raises the table's overall provisioned throughput. This does not fix the actual problem. The actual problem is not a lack of overall capacity. The table's consumed throughput is already well below what is provisioned. The real issue is that one partition key value receives disproportionate traffic. Increasing capacity also raises cost without addressing the root cause. Keyword tip: if consumed throughput stays far below provisioned throughput but throttling still occurs, the fix is key design. The fix is not more capacity.
Add a global secondary index to the table

Explanation

Incorrect. A global secondary index (GSI) allows lookups on non-key attributes. A GSI improves query flexibility. A GSI does not change how the base table's partition key distributes write traffic. A GSI would not resolve the hot partition problem. A GSI also adds extra write capacity cost because DynamoDB must maintain the index. Keyword tip: GSIs solve query access-pattern problems. GSIs do not solve partition key hot-spotting.

This question tests understanding of DynamoDB partition key design. It also tests how hot partitions cause throttling even when a table's overall provisioned throughput is not exhausted. DynamoDB distributes provisioned throughput evenly across partitions. A low-cardinality partition key, such as event date, concentrates traffic on a single partition. This exceeds that partition's per-partition limits and triggers ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors. The best-practice, lowest-cost fix is to increase the effective cardinality of the partition key. A common method is adding a random suffix, known as write sharding. Adding capacity, adding indexes, or adding a buffering layer only treats symptoms. These approaches do not fix the root cause.

In practice: a sports analytics company like Keystone Networks often sees this exact pattern on high-traffic game days, when thousands of event records for the same date are written within a short window. By sharding the partition key with a random suffix, Keystone Networks can spread these writes evenly across partitions and avoid throttling, all without paying for additional provisioned capacity that would sit idle outside of peak game times.
