Question 52Incorrect

Solstice Continental, a weather and climate research agency, relies on the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) within the frontend of its public climate data portal to manage user authentication through AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS). The agency stores satellite imagery and climate visualization files in an Amazon S3 bucket named solstice-continental-climate-assets, distributing them globally through an Amazon CloudFront distribution configured with the S3 bucket as its origin.

The engineering team discovered that the portal's application code currently embeds its IAM role credentials in plaintext within a Python module. To close this security gap, the team wants a mechanism that lets the application obtain temporary credentials at runtime without hardcoding any secrets in the codebase.

What solution would meet these requirements?

Set up a CloudFront function on the distribution. Trigger this function for each viewer request. Move the credentials from the Python file into this function and relocate all SDK calls from the frontend into the function.

Explanation

Incorrect. This option moves the plaintext credentials from the Python file into a CloudFront function. This does not remove the security risk. It only moves the exposed credentials to a different layer of the stack. In addition, CloudFront functions run in a restricted JavaScript runtime. This runtime cannot call other AWS services such as AWS STS. Keyword tip: any option that still copies static credentials into code, no matter where, fails the requirement to remove embedded credentials.
Attach a Lambda@Edge function to the CloudFront distribution. Trigger the function upon each viewer request. Move the credentials from the Python file into this function and move all SDK calls from the frontend into this function.

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda@Edge is the correct compute service for this use case, but this option still hardcodes the plaintext credentials into the function code. It does not use an IAM execution role with AWS STS permissions to get temporary credentials dynamically. Embedding static credentials anywhere in code, even inside a Lambda@Edge function, remains a security risk because the credentials could be exposed through version control or logs. Keyword tip: the correct solution replaces static embedded credentials with an IAM execution role that retrieves temporary credentials from AWS STS at runtime.
Correct answer
Attach a Lambda@Edge function to the CloudFront distribution. Trigger the function upon each viewer request. Give the function's execution role the permissions needed to call AWS STS. Move all SDK calls from the frontend to this function.

Explanation

Correct. Lambda@Edge functions run in a standard Lambda execution environment at CloudFront edge locations. A Lambda@Edge function can be assigned an IAM execution role. If that execution role has permission to call AWS STS, the application can request temporary credentials at runtime instead of storing static credentials in code. This approach meets the security requirement and keeps the authentication logic close to the viewer request. Keyword tip: when a scenario needs the application to call other AWS services, such as AWS STS, or run full SDK logic at the edge, Lambda@Edge is the correct choice, not CloudFront Functions.
Your answer is incorrect
Configure a CloudFront function within the distribution. Trigger the function on each viewer request. Grant the function's execution role the permissions needed to call AWS STS. Move all SDK calls from the frontend to this function.

Explanation

Incorrect. CloudFront Functions are designed only for lightweight, sub-millisecond HTTP request and response changes, such as header rewrites or URL redirects. CloudFront Functions run in a limited JavaScript environment with no network access to other AWS services. CloudFront Functions cannot be granted permissions to call AWS STS or run AWS SDK calls, so this approach is not technically possible. Keyword tip: CloudFront Functions cannot access AWS APIs and cannot use IAM execution roles for service calls; that capability belongs only to Lambda@Edge.

This question tests the difference between Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions for secure credential handling at the edge. Lambda@Edge should be used when the logic needs to call other AWS services, such as AWS STS to obtain temporary credentials, or when the logic needs to run more complex SDK operations. CloudFront Functions are limited to lightweight HTTP request and response changes and have no access to AWS service APIs. The correct approach always replaces static, embedded credentials with an IAM execution role that retrieves short-lived credentials at runtime, instead of simply moving hardcoded secrets to a different execution environment.

Business scenario: Solstice Continental's climate portal delivers real-time forecast dashboards to meteorologists around the world. A leaked credential embedded in the portal's code could expose the agency's internal AWS resources to unauthorized access. By moving the authentication logic to a Lambda@Edge function with an IAM execution role, the agency ensures that temporary credentials are generated automatically for each viewer request. This reduces the risk of credential leakage, even if the frontend code repository is later compromised.

Question 53Incorrect

Lattice Federation needs to prevent data loss when its Internet-of-Things (IoT) sensor network experiences periodic traffic spikes while streaming into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. This state government agency, which monitors public infrastructure sensors across multiple municipalities, relies on continuous telemetry for compliance reporting.

The engineering team notices that the PutRecords API call occasionally fails during these spikes, and the application logs show the following response for a batch write:

  1. HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  2. x-amzn-RequestId: <RequestId>
  3. Content-Type: application/x-amz-json-1.1
  4. Content-Length: <PayloadSizeBytes>
  5. Date: <Date>
  6.  
  7. {
  8.   "FailedRecordCount": 2,
  9.   "Records": [
  10.     {
  11.       "SequenceNumber": "49543463076548007577105092703039560359975228518395012686",
  12.       "ShardId": "shardId-000000000000"
  13.     },
  14.     {
  15.       "ErrorCode": "ProvisionedThroughputExceededException",
  16.       "ErrorMessage": "Rate exceeded for shard shardId-000000000001 in stream exampleStreamName under account 111111111111."
  17.     },
  18.     {
  19.       "ErrorCode": "InternalFailure",
  20.       "ErrorMessage": "Internal service failure."
  21.     }
  22.   ]
  23. }

Which of the following actions should the development team take to resolve this issue? (Select TWO.)

Decrease the number of KCL consumers

Explanation

Incorrect. The Kinesis Client Library (KCL) consumer count affects the read side of a stream, not the write side. The ProvisionedThroughputExceededException error in this scenario comes from PutRecords calls made by producers, not from consumers. Changing the number of KCL consumers has no effect on producer-side throttling. Keyword tip: KCL consumers affect reads through GetRecords, not writes through PutRecords.
Correct selection
Decrease the frequency or size of your requests

Explanation

Correct. A ProvisionedThroughputExceededException error on PutRecords means the write request rate or data volume for a shard exceeds its throughput limit. Reducing the frequency or size of requests lowers the load on the throttled shard. Distributing writes more evenly across shards, or adding shards through resharding, also addresses the root cause. Keyword tip: throughput-exceeded errors are resolved by reducing load or by increasing and redistributing shard capacity, never by increasing load.
Your selection is incorrect
Merge the shards to decrease the number of shards in the stream

Explanation

Incorrect. Merging shards reduces the total number of shards in the stream. Fewer shards means the stream has less total write capacity, not more. Reducing capacity makes ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors more likely, not less. The correct action for a throttled shard is to split shards or redistribute the write load, not merge them. Keyword tip: merging shards lowers capacity, so it is never the fix for a throughput-exceeded error.
Your selection is correct
Use an error retry and exponential backoff mechanism

Explanation

Correct. When the PutRecords API returns a partial failure with the error code ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, AWS recommends retrying the failed records with exponential backoff. Exponential backoff increases the wait time between each retry attempt. This wait time gives the throttled shard time to recover before the next retry. The retry with backoff approach reduces the chance of repeated throttling errors. Keyword tip: whenever a Kinesis or DynamoDB response includes ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, think retry with exponential backoff.
Increase the frequency or size of your requests

Explanation

Incorrect. Increasing the frequency or size of requests sends more data to an already throttled shard. Sending more data to a throttled shard makes the ProvisionedThroughputExceededException error worse. The correct action is to reduce the frequency or size of requests, or to spread the write load across more shards. Keyword tip: never increase load in response to a throughput-exceeded error.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams throughput limits and how to handle partial failures from the PutRecords API. Each shard in a Kinesis data stream supports up to 1,000 records per second and up to 1 MiB per second of write throughput. When a producer exceeds these limits, the affected records receive a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException error, even though the overall PutRecords call still returns an HTTP 200 OK status. The correct remediation reduces the request rate or size, distributes writes evenly across shards using well-chosen partition keys, reshards to add shard capacity when sustained throughput is insufficient, and retries failed records with exponential backoff.

Consider this scenario: Lattice Federation streams sensor telemetry from public infrastructure devices into a single Kinesis data stream, and traffic spikes during peak reporting windows push write traffic past a single shard's throughput limit. The development team adds retry logic with exponential backoff to handle transient ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors, and reduces the request rate on the affected producer until the stream is resharded with additional shards. This combination keeps sensor data flowing without loss during traffic spikes.

Troubleshooting and Optimization
Question 54Correct

Mapleridge Alliance currently hosts its national courier tracking website on Amazon EC2 instances, using an Auto Scaling group to adjust compute resources during shipping volume spikes. Customers across the country now report slow page load times because static content hosted on the EC2 instances takes too long to load, even outside of peak shipping periods.

Which two actions should the company take to improve the website's latency? (Select TWO.)

Your selection is correct
Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution to cache the static content, configuring Amazon S3 as the origin

Explanation

Correct. Amazon CloudFront caches content at edge locations around the world. CloudFront routes each user request to the nearest edge location, which reduces the distance data must travel. Configuring the Amazon S3 bucket as the origin lets CloudFront pull the static content once and then serve cached copies close to users everywhere. Keyword tip: mentions of edge locations, global users, or reducing latency for static content point to CloudFront with S3 as the origin.
Migrate the application to AWS Lambda

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service. AWS Lambda runs application code in response to events. AWS Lambda does not store files, and AWS Lambda cannot serve static content such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or image files directly to users. Keyword tip: if an option moves static assets to a compute-only service, treat that option as a decoy.
Your selection is correct
Transfer the application's static content hosted on the EC2 instances to Amazon S3

Explanation

Correct. Moving static content from the EC2 instances to Amazon S3 separates static asset storage from compute capacity. Amazon S3 stores files reliably and can serve them directly to users. This setup lets the Auto Scaling group manage only application logic, not static file delivery. Keyword tip: static content type (images, CSS, JS, HTML) combined with global latency complaints points to an S3 and CloudFront pattern.
Upgrade the CPU and RAM available to the EC2 instances

Explanation

Incorrect. Upgrading CPU and RAM increases compute power for each EC2 instance. This action helps when a server is overloaded by processing work. The described problem is slow loading of static content, even outside busy periods, which points to network distance as the cause, not server hardware. Keyword tip: hardware upgrades fix compute-bound problems, not geographic or network latency problems.
Double the Auto Scaling group's desired capacity

Explanation

Incorrect. Increasing the Auto Scaling group's desired capacity adds more EC2 instances. More EC2 instances can handle more requests, but adding instances does not reduce the network distance between users and the server. The latency problem happens even during low-traffic periods, so instance count is not the root cause. Keyword tip: latency issues that persist regardless of traffic level point away from scaling capacity as the fix.

This scenario distinguishes compute scaling solutions from content delivery optimization solutions when diagnosing latency problems. Amazon S3 provides durable, scalable storage that is well suited for static files such as images, CSS, and JavaScript. Amazon CloudFront caches those files at edge locations around the world, so each user request travels a shorter distance to reach the content. Auto Scaling and instance upgrades add compute capacity, but adding compute capacity does not reduce network distance, so those actions do not fix latency problems that occur even at low traffic; AWS Lambda cannot serve static content at all, because AWS Lambda is a compute service, not a storage service.

In practice: a national courier company like Mapleridge Alliance serves package tracking pages and shipping label images to customers across many regions. Moving those static assets to Amazon S3 and placing an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket lets customers in distant cities load tracking pages quickly, without their requests traveling back to a single EC2 region every time.

Question 55Correct

Dunmore National needs a way to automatically retry AWS Lambda invocations that fail during asynchronous processing while minimizing operational overhead. The company, a food and beverage producer that asynchronously invokes a Lambda function named dunmore-order-processor to handle incoming order events, has recently experienced occasional errors that result in failed invocations.

A developer wants to store the messages that resulted in failed invocations so that the application can automatically retry processing them.

What should the developer do to accomplish this goal with the LEAST operational overhead?

Configure logging to an Amazon CloudWatch Logs group. Configure Lambda to read failed invocation events from the log group.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon CloudWatch Logs stores log data for observability and debugging, not for message replay. CloudWatch Logs does not provide a built-in mechanism for Lambda to read failed invocation events back for reprocessing. The log entries may also lack the full event payload needed to retry the original request. Keyword tip: when a question describes reading failed events from CloudWatch Logs for retries, recognize this as unsupported, since CloudWatch Logs is not a message queue.
Configure Amazon EventBridge to send the messages to Amazon SNS to initiate the Lambda function again.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon EventBridge can be configured as a Lambda failure destination, and it can forward events to Amazon SNS, which can then invoke the Lambda function again. This chain requires configuring multiple services and rules, which adds more operational overhead than a single SQS dead-letter queue. Keyword tip: a multi-service chain like EventBridge to SNS to Lambda is a valid but heavier solution, not the least-overhead option.
Your answer is correct
Configure a redrive policy on an Amazon SQS queue. Set the dead-letter queue as an event source to the Lambda function.

Explanation

Correct. A redrive policy on an Amazon SQS queue defines a dead-letter queue (DLQ) that receives messages after repeated processing failures. Setting that DLQ as an event source mapping for the Lambda function lets AWS automatically deliver the failed messages back to the function for retry. This approach uses fully managed AWS features and needs no custom code, so it produces the lowest operational overhead. Keyword tip: the phrase "redrive policy" combined with "dead-letter queue as event source" points to the native, low-overhead SQS retry pattern.
Configure an Amazon S3 bucket as a destination for failed invocations. Configure event notifications to trigger the Lambda function to process the events.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 is not a supported failure destination for asynchronous Lambda invocations. Lambda supports Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS, Amazon EventBridge, and another Lambda function as failure destinations. Amazon S3 would require custom event notification wiring that Lambda does not provide natively for this purpose. Keyword tip: if a question proposes Amazon S3 as a native Lambda failure destination, treat it as incorrect, because S3 is not one of the four supported destination types.

This question tests understanding of failure handling for asynchronously invoked AWS Lambda functions. Lambda supports on-failure destinations of Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, and another Lambda function, but not Amazon S3 or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Configuring a redrive policy on an Amazon SQS queue, and then using the resulting dead-letter queue as an event source mapping for the Lambda function, is the simplest and most automated way to capture failed messages and retry them, because it relies entirely on managed AWS behavior with no custom integration code. Chaining services such as EventBridge and SNS can also route failed events back to Lambda, but this adds extra configuration steps and operational overhead compared to the single-queue SQS pattern, so it should only be chosen when the SQS pattern cannot meet a specific routing requirement.

Business scenario: Dunmore National runs an order-processing pipeline where a Lambda function named dunmore-order-processor occasionally fails due to transient downstream errors, such as a temporary database timeout. By attaching an SQS dead-letter queue with a redrive policy and using that queue as the function's event source, Dunmore National ensures failed order events are automatically retried without requiring its developers to build or maintain any additional retry logic.

Question 56Correct

A streaming pipeline writes to an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream provisioned with 20 shards, and CloudWatch metrics confirm that the pipeline runs well below the stream's aggregate throughput limit of 20 MB per second, since it sends only 6 MB per second of data. Everstone Enterprises, a satellite communications provider that uses this stream to ingest telemetry from its network of ground stations, still sees the pipeline frequently throttled with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors.

What is the most likely cause of this behavior?

Metrics are slow to update

Explanation

Incorrect. CloudWatch metric delays are a monitoring visibility issue only. A delay in metric reporting does not cause Kinesis to reject writes. Keyword tip: treat CloudWatch metric lag as an unrelated distractor whenever the question asks about a specific throttling exception like ProvisionedThroughputExceededException.
You have too many shards

Explanation

Incorrect. Having too many shards does not cause write throughput errors by itself. If an account exceeds the Kinesis limit on the number of shards, AWS returns a LimitExceededException, not a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. Keyword tip: LimitExceededException relates to shard count or API limits. ProvisionedThroughputExceededException relates to per-shard throughput.
Your answer is correct
The partition key that you have selected isn't distributed enough

Explanation

Correct. Kinesis Data Streams uses the partition key of each record to select a shard. The stream applies a hashing algorithm to the partition key to make this selection. Each shard has its own fixed write limit of 1 MB per second and 1,000 records per second. If the partition key has low cardinality or an uneven distribution, many records land on the same shard. This creates a hot shard that exceeds its own throughput limit, even though the overall stream utilization stays low. Keyword tip: when the aggregate throughput number looks fine but ProvisionedThroughputExceededException still occurs, suspect a poorly distributed partition key and consider a higher-cardinality key or splitting the hot shard.
The data retention period is too long

Explanation

Incorrect. The data retention period controls how long records stay available for consumption. The default retention period is 24 hours, and it can extend up to 365 days. Retention period settings do not affect write throughput. Retention period settings cannot cause a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException. Keyword tip: link retention period only to data expiration questions, not to write-capacity errors like ProvisionedThroughputExceededException.

This question tests how Amazon Kinesis Data Streams distributes records across shards using the partition key, and why stream-level aggregate metrics can hide per-shard throttling. Each shard has a fixed write capacity of 1 MB per second and 1,000 records per second. A poorly distributed, low-cardinality partition key routes too many records to the same shard. This creates a hot shard that exceeds its own limit and returns ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, even when the overall stream utilization stays low. The correct fix is to choose a partition key with high cardinality and even distribution, and to use shard-level CloudWatch metrics to find and split hot shards or merge cold ones.

Real-world example: Everstone Enterprises, a satellite communications provider, ingests telemetry from its ground stations into a Kinesis Data Stream. If the engineering team partitions records by a low-cardinality field such as satellite region, one region generating more traffic can overload a single shard and trigger throttling errors, even though the overall stream shows low aggregate utilization. Switching to a higher-cardinality partition key, such as a unique ground-station ID, spreads the load evenly across shards and eliminates the throttling.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/key-concepts.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/kinesis-using-sdk-java-resharding-strategies.html

Question 57Incorrect

During a recent surge in delivery volume, engineers noticed that intermittent API throttling was causing the same parcel-status update to be processed more than once, leading to inconsistent tracking records. The affected system belongs to Oakhaven Continental, a national courier and parcel service, whose mobile driver app sends data to a Lambda function-based RESTful API.

Each API request is assigned a unique identifier by the application. The volume of API requests from drivers' mobile devices can vary unpredictably at any time of day. During periods of request throttling, the application might need to retry requests. The API must be able to handle duplicate requests without introducing inconsistencies or losing data.

Which approach should be recommended to meet these requirements?

Persist the unique identifier for each request in an ElastiCache for Memcached cache. Change the Lambda function to check the cache for the identifier before processing the request

Explanation

Incorrect. Memcached does not provide persistence. Memcached does not provide snapshotting or replication either. If a Memcached node fails, all stored identifiers are lost. A lost identifier means a duplicate request can be processed again. Processing a duplicate request again causes data loss and inconsistent records. Keyword tip: Memcached has no persistence or backup, so it is unsuitable whenever durable storage of state is required.
Your answer is incorrect
Persist the unique identifier for each request in an RDS for MySQL table. Change the Lambda function to check the table for the identifier before processing the request

Explanation

Incorrect. An RDS for MySQL table can technically store and check identifiers. However, RDS for MySQL scales mainly by increasing the size of a single instance. This vertical scaling approach becomes a bottleneck under unpredictable, high-volume write traffic. DynamoDB scales horizontally across many partitions and handles massive request rates with consistent single-digit-millisecond latency. Keyword tip: unpredictable or high-volume traffic with strict latency needs points to DynamoDB instead of a relational database like RDS.
Persist the unique identifier for each request in a DynamoDB table. Change the Lambda function to send a client error response when the function receives a duplicate request

Explanation

Incorrect. Returning a client error response for a duplicate request does not meet the requirement to handle retries safely. The application must process retries transparently instead of exposing an error to the client. Rejecting a duplicate request with an error is not the same as ignoring it safely. Keyword tip: idempotent design means silently handling duplicate requests, not returning an error for them.
Correct answer
Persist the unique identifier for each request in a DynamoDB table. Change the Lambda function to check the table for the identifier before processing the request

Explanation

Correct. Storing the unique identifier in a DynamoDB table implements an idempotency pattern. The Lambda function checks the table for the identifier before processing each request. If the identifier already exists, the function skips reprocessing and avoids duplicate side effects. DynamoDB provides durability through continuous backups and point-in-time recovery, so the stored identifier is not lost even during throttling and retries. Keyword tip: DynamoDB plus an identifier lookup before processing is the standard idempotent API pattern for Lambda-backed APIs.

This question tests the idempotency design pattern for serverless APIs. A unique request identifier is stored in a durable, highly scalable data store and checked before processing, which prevents duplicate side effects when a client retries a request after throttling. DynamoDB is the correct choice because it scales horizontally to handle unpredictable traffic spikes, maintains consistent low latency, and provides built-in durability through continuous backups and point-in-time recovery. ElastiCache for Memcached fails this requirement because it has no persistence, and RDS for MySQL fails because it scales vertically and can become a bottleneck under bursty write-heavy traffic.

In practice: A national courier company like Oakhaven Continental processes many delivery-status updates from mobile devices during peak shipping periods, and network retries during throttling can easily create duplicate status updates. By storing each request's unique identifier in DynamoDB and checking for it before processing, Oakhaven Continental ensures that a retried update never creates a duplicate or inconsistent parcel record, even during traffic surges.

https://aws.amazon.com/elasticache/redis-vs-memcached/

Question 58Incorrect

Sablecrest Enterprises, a hospitality and hotel chain, runs its online room-booking platform on a fleet of EC2 instances placed behind an Application Load Balancer. A cloud engineer on the company's platform team notices that the target group reports every instance as unhealthy, yet pasting the private IP address of any instance directly into a browser loads the booking site with no problem at all.

Which two factors could explain why the load balancer marks the instances as unhealthy? (Select TWO.)

Your selection is correct
The security group of the EC2 instances does not allow traffic from the security group of the Application Load Balancer

Explanation

Correct. The load balancer must be able to send traffic to each target on both the listener port and the health check port. If the security group attached to the EC2 instances does not allow inbound traffic from the Application Load Balancer's security group, the health check requests are blocked. The load balancer then reports the targets as unhealthy, even though a browser using an allowed source can still reach the instance directly. Keyword tip: whenever health checks fail but direct access works, verify that the instance security group permits inbound traffic from the load balancer's security group on the health check port.
You need to attach an Elastic IP address to the EC2 instances

Explanation

Incorrect. An Elastic IP address is not required for an EC2 instance to belong to a target group. The Application Load Balancer communicates with target instances using their private IP addresses inside the VPC. Attaching an Elastic IP address has no effect on target health status. Keyword tip: treat Elastic IP addresses as unrelated to target group health checks; this option is a common distractor in load balancer questions.
Your selection is incorrect
The web application has a runtime that is not supported by the Application Load Balancer

Explanation

Incorrect. The Application Load Balancer works at Layer 7. It forwards HTTP or HTTPS requests and runs health checks against a configured path. The load balancer does not check or restrict the programming language or runtime of the backend application. Keyword tip: watch for answer choices that invent a compatibility rule between a load balancer and an application runtime, because no such rule exists.
Correct selection
The route for the health check is misconfigured

Explanation

Correct. The target group has its own health check settings, including a path, a port, and a protocol. If these settings point to a path that does not exist, or use the wrong port or protocol, the load balancer will mark every target unhealthy even though the application itself works. This happens independently of whether a browser can reach the instance directly. Keyword tip: when instances are reachable individually but fail load balancer health checks, check the health check path, port, and protocol first.
The EBS volumes have been improperly mounted

Explanation

Incorrect. The engineer can load the booking site by browsing directly to the instance IP address. This proves the web server and its storage are working correctly. An EBS mounting problem would also break direct access, so this cannot be the cause. Keyword tip: if the application works when reached directly on the instance, rule out any option describing an application-level or storage-level failure.

This question tests the ability to diagnose Application Load Balancer target health check failures when the application itself is confirmed to be working. There are two common root causes for this pattern. First, the health check settings on the target group, meaning the path, port, or protocol, can be misconfigured so the load balancer never receives a valid response. Second, the security group on the EC2 instances can block inbound traffic from the load balancer's security group, so the health check requests never arrive. Both causes produce the same symptom: direct browser access to the instance succeeds, but the load balancer still reports the target as unhealthy. Unrelated factors, such as EBS volume mounting, Elastic IP addresses, or application runtime, do not affect target health and should be ruled out first.

Business scenario: Sablecrest Enterprises depends on its booking platform staying available so guests can reserve rooms without interruption. If the load balancer removes healthy instances from rotation due to a misconfigured health check path or a restrictive security group rule, guest-facing traffic can be routed to too few instances or fail entirely, even though the servers are running correctly. A platform engineer at Sablecrest Enterprises would check the target group health check configuration and the instance security group rules before assuming there is a deeper application problem.

Troubleshooting and Optimization
Question 59Correct

Ridgewood Systems, an agricultural cooperative, runs an Amazon EC2 instance with an IAM instance role attached, granting it read and write access to the S3 bucket named 'ridgewood-harvest-data'. An engineer tests the IAM instance role and confirms that both reads and writes succeed.

The engineer then detaches the IAM instance role from the EC2 instance and tests both operations again. After detaching the role, write operations stop working, but read operations continue to succeed.

What is the most likely cause of this behavior?

The EC2 instance is using cached temporary IAM credentials

Explanation

Incorrect. The engineer removed the IAM instance role from the EC2 instance. After this removal, the EC2 instance metadata service does not hold or serve any valid temporary credentials tied to that role. Any S3 call made after the removal needs a different credential source, and the scenario does not describe one. Keyword tip: instance role removal invalidates the instance's ability to retrieve fresh temporary credentials, so 'cached credentials' cannot explain access that continues to work after removal.
Your answer is correct
The S3 bucket policy authorizes read operations

Explanation

Correct. When an EC2 instance calls Amazon S3, AWS evaluates the combined effect of the IAM identity-based policy attached to the instance role and the S3 bucket policy on the target bucket. AWS grants access if either policy allows the action, as long as no explicit deny exists. After the engineer removes the IAM instance role, the EC2 instance has no IAM identity-based permissions left. Only the bucket policy controls access at that point, and the bucket policy in this scenario allows reads but not writes. Keyword tip: when access continues to work after an IAM role is removed, look for a bucket policy or other resource-based policy that still grants that specific permission.
Removing an instance role from an EC2 instance can take a few minutes before the change becomes active

Explanation

Incorrect. Detaching an IAM instance role from an EC2 instance takes effect immediately. AWS does not apply a delay before the role removal becomes active. This option also does not explain why reads kept working while writes failed. If the role removal were delayed, both reads and writes would still work for a period of time. Keyword tip: watch for distractors that invent a propagation delay for an IAM change that AWS actually applies instantly.
When a read is performed on a bucket, there is a grace period of 5 minutes during which the same read can be repeated without re-evaluation

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS does not have a 5-minute grace period for repeated read requests. AWS evaluates every single API request independently against the current IAM and bucket policies. AWS does not cache or reuse a prior authorization decision for a later request. Keyword tip: treat any option that describes a temporary grace period or caching window for authorization decisions as a fabricated distractor, because AWS access evaluation happens per request.

This question tests how AWS evaluates access when both an IAM identity-based policy and an S3 bucket policy apply to the same request. AWS combines the permissions from the IAM role policy attached to the EC2 instance and the resource-based bucket policy on the S3 bucket. AWS grants an action if either policy allows it, unless an explicit deny exists in either policy. Use an IAM role policy to control what a specific identity, such as an EC2 instance, can do across many resources, and use a bucket policy to control access to one specific bucket regardless of which identity makes the call. When the engineer removes the IAM role, the identity-based permissions disappear, so only the bucket policy remains in effect, which explains why reads kept working and writes stopped.

Practical example: Ridgewood Systems could store daily harvest and yield reports in the 'ridgewood-harvest-data' bucket, using a bucket policy that makes the reports readable by any authorized system across the cooperative's network, while restricting write access to a dedicated EC2-based ingestion service through an IAM role. If an administrator removes that IAM role during a security review, cooperative staff would still be able to read existing harvest reports through the bucket policy, but the ingestion service would lose its ability to upload new data until the role is reattached or an equivalent write grant is added to the bucket policy.

Question 60Correct

An access token must be stored securely so that a transaction-processing application running on Amazon EC2 instances can authenticate and send an automated chat message (via a chat API) whenever an invalid transaction is detected. Ulverstone Ventures, an online gaming company, needs the chat API access token to reach its support team, and the token must be encrypted both at rest and in transit, must be accessible from other AWS accounts, and must require minimal management overhead.

What is the most efficient solution to address this scenario?

Your answer is correct
Leverage AWS Secrets Manager with an AWS KMS customer-managed key to store the access token as a secret and configure a resource-based policy for the secret to allow access from other accounts. Modify the IAM role of the EC2 instances with permissions to access Secrets Manager. Fetch the token from Secrets Manager and then use the decrypted access token to send the message to the chat.

Explanation

Correct. AWS Secrets Manager is built specifically to store and manage secrets such as access tokens. Secrets Manager encrypts each secret at rest using an AWS KMS customer-managed key and encrypts data in transit using TLS. Secrets Manager also supports resource-based policies directly on the secret, so the token can be shared with another AWS account without building extra infrastructure. Secrets Manager integrates with IAM roles for access control, which keeps operational overhead low. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions secrets, cross-account resource-based policies, and low operational overhead together, Secrets Manager is the expected answer.
Leverage SSE-KMS to store the access token as an encrypted object on Amazon S3 and configure a resource-based policy for the S3 bucket to allow access from other accounts. Modify the IAM role of the EC2 instances with permissions to access the S3 object. Fetch the token from S3 and then use the decrypted access token to send the message to the chat.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 bucket policies are a form of resource-based policy, and bucket policies can grant cross-account access. However, storing a sensitive access token as a flat object in S3 is a security anti-pattern, because S3 does not provide secret lifecycle features such as automatic rotation or secret-level access auditing. Keyword tip: avoid storing credentials as plain files or objects, even when encrypted, whenever a dedicated secrets service is available.
Store an AWS KMS encrypted access token in a DynamoDB table and configure a resource-based policy for the DynamoDB table to allow access from other accounts. Modify the IAM role of the EC2 instances with permissions to access the DynamoDB table. Fetch the token from the DynamoDB table and then use the decrypted access token to send the message to the chat.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon DynamoDB does not support resource-based policies for individual items or tables in a way that grants cross-account access to a single token. Storing an access token in a general-purpose database is also a security anti-pattern because DynamoDB was not built for secret management. A dedicated secrets management service is a better fit for this requirement. Keyword tip: DynamoDB has no resource-based policy support at the item level and is not a secrets management service.
Leverage AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with an AWS KMS customer-managed key to store the access token as a SecureString parameter and configure a resource-based policy for the parameter to allow access from other accounts. Modify the IAM role of the EC2 instances with permissions to access Parameter Store. Fetch the token from Parameter Store using the with-decryption flag and then use the decrypted access token to send the message to the chat.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store does not support resource-based policies on individual parameters. Without a resource-based policy, Parameter Store cannot directly grant another AWS account access to a single parameter. Parameter Store does offer parameter policies, but parameter policies control tasks like expiration on advanced parameters, not cross-account sharing. Keyword tip: remember that Parameter Store lacks resource-based policies, while Secrets Manager supports them directly on each secret.

This question tests the ability to select the correct AWS service for storing a sensitive secret that must be encrypted at rest and in transit, shared across AWS accounts, and managed with low operational overhead. AWS Secrets Manager meets all three requirements because it supports resource-based policies directly on each secret, encrypts the secret with AWS KMS, and integrates with IAM for access control. Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB can both encrypt data, but neither service is designed as a secrets store, and DynamoDB does not support resource-based policies at the item level. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store encrypts SecureString parameters with AWS KMS, but Parameter Store does not support resource-based policies, so Parameter Store cannot grant cross-account access to a single parameter without extra IAM setup.

Business scenario: Ulverstone Ventures, an online gaming company, runs a transaction-processing application on Amazon EC2 instances. When the application detects an invalid transaction, the application must send an automated chat alert through a chat API. The chat API access token must stay encrypted, must be shared with a partner AWS account that manages the support tooling, and must require minimal ongoing maintenance. AWS Secrets Manager satisfies all of these requirements in a single managed service.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/auth-and-access_examples.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/parameter-store-policies.html

Question 61Incorrect

A recent internal audit uncovered several cases where supply-credit transfers between field volunteers left one volunteer's account debited without the paired volunteer's account being credited, creating inconsistent aid-distribution records. Greystone Cooperative, a nonprofit disaster-relief organization that coordinates emergency response teams across flood- and hurricane-prone regions, runs a milestone-based rewards program: when a volunteer reaches a mission-completion milestone tracked on an internal leaderboard, the volunteer earns a supply credit that can be redeemed directly or transferred to another volunteer.

The engineering team at Greystone Cooperative needs to guarantee that every transfer is captured in the database so that both volunteers' records are either updated successfully with the new supply-credit balances, or left completely unchanged, with no partial updates. Which of the following solutions represent the best-fit options to meet the requirements for the given use case? (Select TWO.)

Your selection is incorrect
Perform DynamoDB read and write operations with the ConsistentRead parameter set to true

Explanation

Incorrect. The ConsistentRead parameter controls whether a DynamoDB read operation returns the most recent write, called strong consistency, or possibly older data, called eventual consistency. The ConsistentRead parameter only affects read operations. The ConsistentRead parameter gives no guarantee that multiple write operations happen together as one atomic unit. Keyword tip: ConsistentRead affects read freshness only; do not confuse ConsistentRead with DynamoDB Transactions.
Use the Amazon Athena transactional read and write APIs on the Greystone Cooperative volunteer-credits table items as a single, all-or-nothing operation

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Athena is a serverless query service. Amazon Athena analyzes data stored in Amazon S3 using standard SQL. Amazon Athena does not manage live application records and has no transactional API for updating table items such as the volunteer-credits table described in this scenario. Keyword tip: Amazon Athena is for ad hoc analytics on data in Amazon S3, not for atomic updates to operational records.
Your selection is correct
Complete both operations on Amazon RDS for MySQL in a single transaction block

Explanation

Correct. Amazon RDS for MySQL is a managed relational database. Amazon RDS for MySQL fully supports ACID-compliant transactions. Wrapping the debit from one volunteer's record and the credit to another volunteer's record inside a single transaction block, using BEGIN and then COMMIT or ROLLBACK, makes sure both updates succeed together or neither update happens. Keyword tip: the phrase "transaction block" combined with a relational database like RDS or MySQL signals classic ACID transaction support.
Complete both operations on Amazon Redshift in a single transaction block

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse service. Amazon Redshift is built for large-scale analytical queries, not for real-time transactional updates. Amazon Redshift does not support atomic, all-or-nothing transaction blocks across multiple rows for operational updates like the volunteer supply-credit transfer described here. Keyword tip: if the scenario mentions a data warehouse or large-scale analytics, think Amazon Redshift, not transactional atomicity.
Correct selection
Use the DynamoDB transactional read and write APIs on the Greystone Cooperative volunteer-credits table items as a single, all-or-nothing operation

Explanation

Correct. DynamoDB Transactions provide the TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems APIs. These APIs group multiple operations across one or more tables into a single, all-or-nothing atomic unit. This atomic unit gives ACID guarantees, so the supply-credit debit and the supply-credit credit either both succeed or both fail, leaving the volunteer-credits table in a consistent state. Keyword tip: the phrase "all-or-nothing across multiple items or tables" in a DynamoDB context points directly to DynamoDB Transactions.

This question tests the ability to match a transactional-atomicity requirement to the correct AWS database service and API. Use a relational database transaction block, such as an RDS transaction, when the data lives in a relational schema and needs ACID guarantees across multiple row updates. Use DynamoDB Transactions, through TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems, when the data lives in DynamoDB tables and needs coordinated, all-or-nothing changes across multiple items or tables. Amazon Redshift and Amazon Athena are built for analytical querying, not for atomic operational updates, and the DynamoDB ConsistentRead parameter only controls read freshness, not write atomicity.

Practical example: Greystone Cooperative could store volunteer supply-credit balances in a DynamoDB table and use TransactWriteItems whenever a volunteer transfers a credit to a teammate, guaranteeing that the sender's balance decreases and the recipient's balance increases in one atomic step, even during a surge of transfers after a large-scale disaster response.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/transactions.html
https://aws.amazon.com/relational-database/

Question 62Correct

The network operations team at Solstice Networks, an industrial manufacturing company that runs automated production-line monitoring across several plants, is configuring access to an Amazon EC2 instance that hosts a web-based equipment-status dashboard. A newly onboarded team member configured a new security group to permit incoming HTTP traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 and left the default outbound rules unchanged.

The team also configured a custom Network Access Control List (NACL) associated with the instance's subnet to permit incoming HTTP traffic from 0.0.0.0/0, and also left the default outbound rules unchanged for the NACL.

Which of the following solutions should be suggested if the EC2 instance needs to accept and respond to requests from the internet?

Outbound rules need to be configured both on the security group and on the NACL for sending responses to the internet gateway

Explanation

Incorrect. Security groups are stateful. A stateful firewall tracks each connection automatically. When a security group allows an inbound request, the security group also allows the matching return traffic without needing a separate outbound rule. The NACL is the piece that needs an explicit outbound rule for the ephemeral port range, not the security group. Keyword tip: if an option describes adding outbound rules to a security group just to allow response traffic, treat it as a distractor, because security groups handle return traffic automatically.
Your answer is correct
An outbound rule must be added to the Network ACL (NACL) to allow the response to be sent to the client on the ephemeral port range

Explanation

Correct. Network ACLs are stateless. A stateless firewall does not track connections, so the NACL must have separate rules for inbound traffic and outbound traffic. The client sends its request from a randomly assigned source port in the ephemeral range, which is ports 1024 through 65535. The EC2 instance sends its response back to that same ephemeral port. Because the custom NACL only has an inbound rule for HTTP, the response traffic to the ephemeral port range is blocked until an outbound rule is added for that range. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions a custom NACL and asks how to complete a request-response cycle, the missing piece is almost always an outbound rule for the ephemeral port range.
An outbound rule on the security group has to be configured to allow the response to be sent to the client on the HTTP port

Explanation

Incorrect. Security groups are stateful. Because the security group already allows the inbound HTTP request, the security group automatically allows the matching outbound response traffic. No additional outbound rule for the HTTP port is needed on the security group. Keyword tip: statefulness is the defining trait of security groups, and it is the direct contrast to the stateless behavior of NACLs.
The configuration is complete on the EC2 instance for accepting and responding to requests

Explanation

Incorrect. The custom NACL in this scenario allows inbound HTTP traffic, but the custom NACL does not include an outbound rule for the ephemeral port range that the client uses to receive the response. Without that outbound rule, the NACL blocks the response, and the configuration is incomplete. Keyword tip: a custom NACL denies all traffic by default until an administrator adds explicit rules in both directions, unlike the default NACL, which allows all traffic in both directions.

This question tests the difference between stateful and stateless traffic filtering in an Amazon VPC. A security group is stateful, so when a security group allows an inbound request on a given port, the security group also allows the matching outbound response automatically, with no extra outbound rule required. A NACL is stateless, so a NACL requires separate, explicit rules for inbound traffic and outbound traffic. Because a client's response traffic targets the client's ephemeral port rather than the original service port, a custom NACL must include an outbound rule that allows traffic to the ephemeral port range, which is ports 1024 through 65535. When troubleshooting connectivity issues in a VPC, check both layers in order: first confirm the security group allows the inbound service port, then confirm the custom NACL allows both inbound traffic to the service port and outbound traffic to the ephemeral port range.

Applied example: Solstice Networks hosts an equipment-status dashboard on an EC2 instance so that plant managers can check production-line health from outside the corporate network. The network operations team already configured a security group and a custom NACL to allow inbound HTTP traffic from any address, but plant managers report that the dashboard never loads. The team traces the problem to the custom NACL, which is missing an outbound rule for the ephemeral port range, and adding that rule restores the connection without requiring any change to the security group.

References:

https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/resolve-connection-sg-acl-inbound/
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html#nacl-ephemeral-ports

Domain
Troubleshooting and Optimization
Question 63Correct

Wrenfield Foundation, a point-of-sale software vendor headquartered in Austin, stores sensitive payment transaction logs in an Amazon S3 bucket named wrenfield-pos-transactions, which is encrypted at rest using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). A developer at Wrenfield Foundation must guarantee that every user across the company's multiple AWS accounts who has been granted the S3 GetObject permission can retrieve objects from this bucket only over an encrypted connection.

Which solution enforces this requirement with the least operational overhead?

Configure a resource-based policy on the S3 bucket to allow access when a request has the condition "aws:SecureTransport": "false"

Explanation

Incorrect. An Allow statement that triggers only when aws:SecureTransport is false would grant access to insecure HTTP requests. This is the opposite of the required security outcome. Keyword tip: always check whether a policy statement uses Allow or Deny with the aws:SecureTransport condition, because swapping them reverses the intended enforcement completely.
Configure a resource-based policy on the KMS key to allow access when a request has the condition "aws:SecureTransport": "false"

Explanation

Incorrect. A KMS key policy controls who can perform cryptographic operations on the key, such as Decrypt or GenerateDataKey. It does not control whether the network connection used to call S3 GetObject is encrypted. This option also uses Allow instead of Deny, which would permit insecure requests rather than block them. Keyword tip: enforcing transport security for S3 object downloads belongs in the S3 bucket policy, not the KMS key policy.
Configure a resource-based policy on the KMS key to deny access when a request has the condition "aws:SecureTransport": "false"

Explanation

Incorrect. This option correctly uses Deny, but it applies the condition to the KMS key policy instead of the S3 bucket policy. The KMS key policy governs access to cryptographic operations on the key itself. It has no effect on the transport protocol used when a client calls S3 GetObject. Keyword tip: if a scenario asks about the transport protocol for S3 API calls, the KMS key policy is never the correct location for the fix; use the S3 bucket resource policy instead.
Your answer is correct
Configure a resource-based policy on the S3 bucket to deny access when a request has the condition "aws:SecureTransport": "false"

Explanation

Correct. A Deny statement in the S3 bucket policy that triggers on the condition aws:SecureTransport equal to false blocks any request made over plain HTTP. This forces every caller, including users from other AWS accounts who have GetObject permission, to use HTTPS with TLS. This approach works across accounts because it is enforced at the resource level on the wrenfield-pos-transactions bucket, not at the identity level. Keyword tip: when a question asks to enforce encryption in transit on S3 across multiple accounts, look for a bucket policy Deny statement combined with the condition aws:SecureTransport equal to false.

This question tests the use of the aws:SecureTransport global condition key inside an S3 bucket resource-based policy to enforce encryption in transit. A Deny statement conditioned on aws:SecureTransport equal to false blocks every HTTP request while allowing HTTPS requests to proceed, and this rule applies to any caller regardless of which AWS account they belong to, since it is enforced on the resource rather than on individual identities. An Allow statement with the same condition produces the opposite effect and must always be treated as incorrect for this type of requirement. KMS key policies control access to cryptographic operations on the key, such as Decrypt, and cannot enforce which transport protocol a client uses to call an S3 API operation, so they are never the correct location for this control.

Use case: A point-of-sale software vendor like Wrenfield Foundation stores transaction logs from many merchant accounts in a shared S3 bucket. Adding a Deny statement with the aws:SecureTransport condition to the bucket policy ensures that every merchant account with read access retrieves that data only over TLS, which helps Wrenfield Foundation meet payment card industry data protection requirements without having to configure encryption in transit separately in each connected AWS account.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-bucket-policies.html

Question 64Correct

Solstice Cooperative, a ride-sharing platform, runs a fleet-dispatch system that uses several Amazon SQS queues to coordinate ride requests between drivers and riders across its service area. After reviewing the monthly AWS bill, a developer on the platform team notices that the cost of using Amazon SQS has increased substantially after creating new queues.

However, the developer knows that the queue clients do not generate a lot of traffic and are frequently receiving empty responses from ReceiveMessage calls.

Which of the following actions should the developer take to address this issue?

Decrease DelaySeconds

Explanation

Incorrect. DelaySeconds controls how long a message stays hidden from consumers after it is added to the queue. This setting applies at message submission time, not at retrieval time. Changing DelaySeconds does not change how often ReceiveMessage calls return empty results, so it does not reduce the request costs described in the scenario. Keyword tip: DelaySeconds delays message visibility when a message is written to the queue; it does not control polling behavior or polling costs.
Increase the VisibilityTimeout

Explanation

Incorrect. VisibilityTimeout controls how long a message stays hidden from other consumers after a consumer has retrieved it. This setting exists to prevent duplicate processing before the message is deleted. VisibilityTimeout does not affect how often ReceiveMessage calls return empty results, so increasing it does not reduce the cost caused by empty polling responses. Keyword tip: VisibilityTimeout solves duplicate message processing, not empty-poll billing.
Use a FIFO queue

Explanation

Incorrect. FIFO queues exist to preserve strict message ordering and provide exactly-once processing. This purpose is unrelated to the cost problem described in the scenario. FIFO queues do not reduce empty responses, and they typically cost more than standard queues because of their added guarantees. Keyword tip: choose a FIFO queue when a scenario requires ordering or deduplication, not when the goal is reducing polling cost.
Your answer is correct
Use long polling

Explanation

Correct. Amazon SQS supports two ways to retrieve messages: short polling and long polling. Short polling is the default. With short polling, Amazon SQS sends a response immediately, even when no messages are available. Each of these empty responses is still a billable request. Long polling makes Amazon SQS wait until at least one message is available, up to a maximum wait time of 20 seconds, before it sends a response. This removes most empty responses and lowers the number of billable requests. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes low-traffic queues, frequent empty responses, and rising SQS costs, long polling (setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds to a value greater than 0) is the fix.

This question tests understanding of Amazon SQS polling mechanisms and how they affect cost. Short polling is the default mode. With short polling, Amazon SQS returns a response immediately even when no messages are available, and each of these empty responses is a billable request. Long polling waits for a message to arrive, up to 20 seconds, before it sends a response, which greatly reduces the number of empty responses and lowers cost for low-traffic queues. VisibilityTimeout and DelaySeconds control message visibility timing for consumers and producers, but neither one affects polling cost, and FIFO queues address ordering and deduplication needs rather than cost efficiency. When a scenario describes unexpected SQS cost increases tied to frequent empty responses on low-traffic queues, long polling is the correct remedy.

Real-world example: Solstice Cooperative's dispatch service uses SQS queues to pass ride-matching events between microservices, but during off-peak hours, ride volume drops and consumer clients still poll continuously, generating mostly empty responses that Solstice Cooperative still pays for. By enabling long polling on these queues, the platform team reduces the number of billable empty requests during low-traffic periods without changing how ride events are processed, cutting the SQS bill while keeping dispatch latency acceptable.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-short-and-long-polling.html

Question 65Correct

Real-time sensor and transaction telemetry from thousands of point-of-sale terminals is being sent through the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) into an application built on Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Pinegrove Regional, a point-of-sale software vendor supporting retail chains across the Midwest, depends on this pipeline to process terminal events, but the application has stopped processing data because of a ProvisionedThroughputExceeded exception.

Which of the following actions would help address this issue? (Select TWO.)

Use Kinesis enhanced fan-out for Kinesis Data Streams

Explanation

Incorrect. Enhanced fan-out gives each consumer of a stream a dedicated read throughput pipeline, so multiple consumers can read from the stream in parallel without competing for read capacity. Enhanced fan-out has no effect on write (PUT) capacity limits, and the ProvisionedThroughputExceeded exception in this scenario is triggered by write capacity, not read capacity. Keyword tip: enhanced fan-out is a consumer-side read throughput feature, not a producer-side write throughput feature.
Use Amazon Kinesis Agent instead of the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) for sending data to Kinesis Data Streams

Explanation

Incorrect. Kinesis Agent is an alternative data producer tool to KPL. Switching producer tools does not change the throughput capacity of the underlying stream. The ProvisionedThroughputExceeded exception happens because of shard-level capacity limits, not because of the producer library used. Changing the producer tool does not fix this problem. Keyword tip: a change to producer-side tooling never fixes a shard capacity problem.
Use Amazon SQS instead of Kinesis Data Streams

Explanation

Incorrect. Migrating to Amazon SQS does not fix the root cause of the problem. The root cause is the throughput capacity of the existing Kinesis Data Stream. Moving to SQS would also require rebuilding the entire consumer application, and SQS does not support the ordered, real-time processing pattern that Kinesis Data Streams was chosen for. Keyword tip: switching to a different service is a distractor when the real fix is scaling or adding backoff logic within the current service.
Your selection is correct
Increase the number of shards within the data stream to provide enough capacity

Explanation

Correct. If the elevated input rate is sustained rather than temporary, increasing the number of shards raises the stream's overall read and write capacity. More shards give the stream enough throughput for PUT calls to succeed consistently. Keyword tip: the shard count directly sets the throughput ceiling of a Kinesis Data Stream.
Your selection is correct
Configure the data producer to retry with an exponential backoff

Explanation

Correct. When a ProvisionedThroughputExceeded exception happens because of a temporary spike in the stream's input rate, configuring the producer to retry with an exponential backoff lets the PUT requests succeed once the spike ends. Exponential backoff increases the wait time between each retry attempt, which reduces pressure on the shard while the spike is still active. Keyword tip: exponential backoff is the standard fix for transient throttling errors.

This question tests understanding of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams throughput limits and how to respond correctly to a ProvisionedThroughputExceeded exception. A stream's write and read capacity is set by its number of shards. When PUT calls exceed that capacity, the correct fix depends on whether the spike in traffic is temporary or sustained. For a temporary spike, the producer should retry with exponential backoff, which spaces out retry attempts until the spike passes. For a sustained increase in traffic, the stream needs more shards, since resharding raises the overall throughput ceiling. Changing the producer library, switching to a different messaging service, or enabling enhanced fan-out for consumers does not solve the underlying write-capacity constraint, because none of these actions change how many write operations the shards can accept per second.

Use case: Pinegrove Regional processes terminal event data from point-of-sale devices at many retail locations at once. During a regional promotion, transaction volume from terminals can spike sharply within minutes. Pinegrove Regional's engineering team configures exponential backoff on the producer for short bursts and increases the shard count ahead of planned high-volume events, so the ingestion pipeline keeps accepting terminal data without dropped or delayed transactions.

References:

https://aws.amazon.com/kinesis/data-streams/
https://aws.amazon.com/kinesis/data-streams/faqs/
